basicPropertyValues.val:
The Compendium is popularly referred to as the "Gold Book", in recognition of the contribution of the late Victor Gold, who initiated work on the first edition. It is one of the series of IUPAC "Colour Books" on chemical nomenclature, terminology, symbols and units (see the list of source documents), and collects together terminology definitions from IUPAC recommendations already published in Pure and Applied Chemistry and in the other Colour Books.

Terminology definitions published by IUPAC are drafted by international committees of experts in the appropriate chemistry sub-disciplines, and ratified by IUPAC's Interdivisional Committee on Terminology, Nomenclature and Symbols (ICTNS). In this edition of the Compendium these IUPAC-approved definitions are supplemented with some definitions from ISO and from the International Vocabulary of Basic and General Terms in Metrology; both these sources are recognised by IUPAC as authoritative. The result is a collection of nearly 7000 terms, with authoritative definitions, spanning the whole range of chemistry.

The API can be accessed [here](https://goldbook.iupac.org/pages/api)
IUPAC Gold Book Compendium of Chemical Terminology

comments: The definition was coined by the Working Party on Analytical Chemistry (WPAC) of the Federation of European Chemical Societies (FECS) and is known as the "Edinburgh Definition".
The term "analytical science" was coined in 1998 to emphasize the impact of informatics on analytical chemistry.

basicPropertyValues.val: Scientific discipline that develops and applies strategies, instruments, and procedures to obtain information on the composition and nature of matter in space and time.

comments: An additive matrix effect affects the intercept, not the slope, of a linear calibration curve.
The effect is sometimes termed "translational matrix effect" or "background interference".

basicPropertyValues.val: Matrix effect that is independent of the measured quantity value of the measurand.

comments: An analytical run may comprise measurements on one or more reference materials, blank materials, quality control materials, and analytical samples.

basicPropertyValues.val: Set of measurements of the same quantity performed under repeatability conditions of measurement.

comments: In VIM 4.2, this concept is termed "blank indication" with "background indication" as an alternate term. However, since blank indication refers to the explicit use of a blank material in analytical chemistry, it should be distinguished from the concept "background indication".

basicPropertyValues.val: Indication obtained from a phenomenon, body, or substance similar to the one under investigation but for which a quantity of interest is supposed not to be present or is not contributing to the indication.

comments: A blank indication may be subtracted from an indication, or, in the case of a transmittance measurement, the indication is divided by the blank indication.
The blank indication and the indication must be of the same kind of quantity.

basicPropertyValues.val: Step in a measurement procedure in which the effect of a blank indication is removed from an indication.

comments: In VIM 4.2, "background indication" is given as an alternate term for "blank indication". However, in analytical chemistry these terms refer to different concepts.

basicPropertyValues.val: Indication obtained from a sample of blank material under the measurement conditions for the measurand.

comments: A blank material to which a relevant component has been added is often termed "spiked blank" or "fortified blank". Compare spike, internal standard, and measurement procedure with standard addition.
If the term "blank" is used, for example, to denote blank indication or the related blank value or blank correction, this must be clarified by the context.
Terms such as "solvent blank", "reagent blank", or "matrix blank" are often used to specify the type of blank material.
Testing, processing, and measurement of blank materials are nearly always an essential part of chemical analysis and may be part of quality assurance and quality control.
The concept may be extended to more than one analyte.

The term "procedure (or procedural) blank" is often used to denote a material that is carried through the entire measurement procedure. Terms such as "field blank", "calibration blank", and "instrument blank" refer to materials handled in specific parts of the measurement procedure.

basicPropertyValues.val: Material which contains no, or as little as possible, of the analyte of interest used in measurement to establish a blank indication.

comments: Calibration certificates are often valid for a stated period of time, although this is not stipulated in ISO/IEC 17025.
The authority of the organization issuing the document comes from its demonstrated technical competence.

The document may include a statement describing the calibration procedure and the calibrators (calibrants) applied along with the calibration curve, calibration diagram, or other presentations of the calibration.

basicPropertyValues.val: Document issued by a technically competent organization providing information about a calibration.

comments: Guidelines for the determination of calibration intervals of measuring systems are given in ILAC-G24.
ISO 14532 refers to a period "between routine calibrations".

basicPropertyValues.val: Time period between calibrations over which the performance of the measuring system may be expected to meet specified requirements.

comments: In this definition, "traceability" covers both metrological traceability of a measurement result and examination traceability but not object traceability. Similarly, "uncertainty" covers measurement uncertainty and examination uncertainty.

basicPropertyValues.val: Property value of a reference material, accompanied by statements of associated uncertainty and traceability and identified as a certified property value in the reference material certificate.

comments: Purity can be estimated as \(1 - \sum_{j=1}^{j=N} f_{j}\), where \(f_{j}\) denotes fractions of the same type (mass fraction, amount of substance fraction or number fraction) of all other components \(j = 1, \dots, N\). If the contributions are expressed as mass fractions, this estimation is sometimes termed "mass balance".
Purity is usually related to a major component. The other components are termed "impurities".
The numerical quantity value of purity is often expressed as per cent or per mille.
The quantity, component, and system must be specified.

basicPropertyValues.val: Mass (amount of substance or number of entities) of a specified component divided by the mass (amount of substance or number of entities, respectively) of the system.

comments: A consensus property value could, through appropriate actions, become a certified property value; this is in analogy to the certification of a reference material.
A consensus property value is an example of assigned value.
A consensus property value may be obtained in a material-certification study or by agreement between appropriate organizations or experts.

The consensus property value, when it is a value of a unitary quantity, may be expressed as a mean, median, or mode, and is then termed "consensus mean", "consensus median", or "consensus mode", respectively. The mode and the median also apply for ordinal quantities and the mode applies for nominal properties.

The term "consensus value" is typically used to describe estimates of a measure of location, such as mean value, median or mode, and dispersion derived from results reported by participants in a proficiency testing round (see participant in an interlaboratory comparison), but may also be used to refer to values derived from results of a specified subset of such results or, for example, from a number of laboratories chosen for their expertise for the particular analysis. See performance score and standard deviation for proficiency assessment.

basicPropertyValues.val: Property value derived from a collection of results.

comments: A conventional quantity value is generally accepted as being associated with a suitably small measurement uncertainty, which might be zero.
In quality assurance and quality control in chemistry, a conventional quantity value, which may be a consensus property value, is often termed "assigned value".
Sometimes a conventional quantity value is an estimate of a true quantity value.

basicPropertyValues.val: Quantity value attributed by agreement to a quantity for a given purpose.

comments: Another important concept in characterizing the capability of detection of measurement procedures is the limit of detection.
In some European legislations, the term "decision limit" (denoted as CCα) is used for the concept 'critical value'.
The critical value is chosen to give a probability α (usually 0.05) of a measured quantity value exceeding the critical value when the component is absent.
The critical value is usually considered to be a characteristic of a particular measurement procedure performed in a particular laboratory.
The detection decision is made by comparing a measured quantity value with the critical value.
The quantity measured is usually a mass fraction or a concentration but can also be, for example, a mass or an amount of substance.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measured quantity value for a quantity of a component in a material, above which the component is declared to be present.

comments: "Determination" is a superordinate concept of measurement and examination, and so, the term "determination" should not be used when "measurement" or "examination" applies.
"Determination" is a term in general usage and often implies a human decision.
ISO 9000 defines determination as "activity to find out one or more characteristics and their characteristic values".

basicPropertyValues.val: Set of operations that are carried out on an object in order to provide qualitative or quantitative information about this object.
Component of the matrix that embodies an influence quantity.

comments: "Intralaboratory precision" or "within-laboratory precision" is sometimes used as a synonym of intermediate measurement precision.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement precision under intermediate precision conditions of measurement.

comments: Measurement bias in analytical chemistry may be considered to include run bias, laboratory bias, and measurement procedure bias.

basicPropertyValues.val: Contribution to measurement bias that is attributed to systematic effects on measurement results made in a laboratory.

comments: If the LLOQ is estimated as a multiple of the standard deviation of measured values of a blank material (or one spiked with a small aliquot of the component) obtained under repeatability conditions of measurement, it is important to document the multiplication factor, which may be 5, 6, or 10, applied so that different values stated for the LLOQ can be compared.
The quantity measured is usually a mass fraction or a concentration but can also be for example, a mass or an amount of substance.
The requirement can, for example, be a standard deviation under repeatability conditions of measurement or a measurement uncertainty.

The smallest and largest measured quantity values correspond to the lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) and the upper limit of quantification (ULOQ), respectively. The interval between the LLOQ and ULOQ is the working interval.

basicPropertyValues.val: Smallest or largest measured quantity value, obtained by a given measurement procedure, which fulfils a requirement of fitness for purpose.

comments: Linearity of a measuring system should not be confused with linearity of calibration.
The linearity of a measuring system is assessed during procedure validation.
The set of measured quantity values for which linearity of a measuring system applies is usually termed "linear interval" or "linear range".

basicPropertyValues.val: Ability of a measuring system to provide measured quantity values that are directly proportional to the quantity value of the measurand.

comments: Calibration linearity should not be confused with linearity of a measuring system.
Linearity of calibration is assessed during procedure validation.

Linearity of calibration may be expressed by measures of agreement (for example, correlation coefficient) or deviation (for example, standard error of regression), obtained by regression of calibration data or assessed from a residual plot.

The concept applies to calibration functions of any mathematical form. The term "linearity" is historical and refers to a time when calibration graphs were constructed on paper and were invariably considered to be linear.

basicPropertyValues.val: Closeness of agreement between indications obtained using calibrators in the first step of a calibration and indications predicted by the calibration function for the calibrators’ reference quantity values.

comments: A material is said to be homogeneous with respect to a specified quantity if the quantity values measured using aliquots of a specified size do not fall outside a specified interval. See minimum sample size.
Detailed guidance for the assessment of homogeneity of reference materials is given in ISO Guide 35.

In the homogeneity study of a candidate reference material, it is distinguished whether the analytical samples are taken from different supply units or from a single supply unit ("termed between-bottle homogeneity" or "within-bottle homogeneity", respectively).
Inhomogeneity is a source of measurement uncertainty.

basicPropertyValues.val: Uniform structure or composition of a material with respect to one or more specified properties.

comments: The measurement unit of material recovery is the measurement unit of the quantity related to the specified component divided by the unit of the quantity describing the system. When these units are the same, material recovery may be expressed as a percentage, and the quantity specified.
The term "recovery" is also used to describe a recovered quantity value ratio. Therefore, the term "recovery" should not be used without qualification unless the meaning is clear from the context.

basicPropertyValues.val: Mass (volume, amount of substance) of a specified component isolated from a system divided by the mass (volume, amount of substance) of the system prior to isolation.

comments: A material is said to be stable with respect to a specified property if its measured or examined property value does not fall outside a specified interval during storage under specified conditions over a specified period of time.
A reference material is assessed for the stability of an embodied property under conditions of transport ("short-term stability") and storage ("long-term stability").
The term "stability" is also used for stability of a measuring instrument or process (see control limit).

The variation of the property value over time adds a contribution to the uncertainty budget or the examination uncertainty, as applicable. Regarding the assessment of stability of the reference material, detailed guidance is given in ISO Guide 35.

basicPropertyValues.val: Constancy of a property of a material over time.

comments: A measurement procedure can include a statement concerning a target measurement uncertainty.
A measurement procedure is usually documented in sufficient detail to enable an operator to perform a measurement.
An authorized measurement procedure is sometimes termed "standard operating procedure" (SOP) or "recommended operating procedure" (ROP).
In ISO/IEC 17025, the term "method" is used for measurement procedure. "Examination procedure" is defined for medical laboratories.
Measurement procedures in chemistry can be structured according to ISO 78-2 or Annex A of the Eurachem Guide "The Fitness for Purpose of Analytical Methods".
The historical term "assay" is now largely obsolete as a synonym for metrological terms such as measurement procedure but still used in composite terms, for example, immunoassay and bioassay.

basicPropertyValues.val: Detailed description of a measurement according to one or more measurement principles and to a given measurement method, based on a measurement model and including any calculation to obtain a measurement result.

comments: Contributions to measurement procedure bias are calculated during procedure validation.
Measurement bias in analytical chemistry may be considered to include run bias, laboratory bias, and measurement procedure bias.
Measurement procedure bias covers instrumental bias.

basicPropertyValues.val: Contribution to measurement bias that is attributed to systematic effects on measurement results made according to a measurement procedure.

comments: A measurement procedure with standard addition provides an unbiased measurement result if there is a multiplicative matrix effect.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement procedure in which indications are obtained for an analytical sample as well as for analytical samples with addition(s) of a measurement standard.

comments: Relevant statistical terms are given in ISO 5725-1 and ISO 5725-2.
The term "interlaboratory precision" or "between-laboratory precision" is sometimes used as a synonym of measurement reproducibility.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement precision under reproducibility conditions of measurement.

comments: As required by the Mutual Recognition Arrangement (MRA) of the International Committee for Weights and Measures (CIPM), through which national metrology institutes demonstrate the international equivalence of their measurement standards, the concept "degree of equivalence" is applied in special interlaboratory comparisons termed "key comparisons". The degree of equivalence of each national measurement standard is expressed quantitatively by two terms: its deviation from the reference quantity value of the key comparison and the measurement uncertainty of this deviation (at a level of confidence of approximately 95 %). See also: metrological equivalence of measurement results.

Correlation between the measurements influences metrological compatibility of measurement results. If the measurements are completely uncorrelated, the standard measurement uncertainty of their difference is equal to the root square sum of their standard measurement uncertainties, while it is lower for positive covariance or higher for negative covariance.

Metrological compatibility of measurement results replaces the traditional concept of "staying within the error", as it represents the criterion for deciding whether two measurement results refer to the same measurand or not. If in a set of measurements of a measurand, thought to be constant, a measurement result is not compatible with the others, either the measurement was not correct (for example, its measurement uncertainty, was assessed as being too small), or the measured quantity changed between measurements.

basicPropertyValues.val: Property of a set of measurement results for a specified measurand, such that the absolute value of the difference of any pair of measured quantity values from two different measurement results is smaller than some chosen multiple of the standard measurement uncertainty of that difference.

comments: Measurement results are either metrologically equivalent or they are not.

basicPropertyValues.val: Property of two or more measurement results for a given measurand which have metrological compatibility of measurement results, so that they are each acceptable for the same specified intended use.

comments: Examples of documentation include a measurement procedure, product information sheets (see reference material), and reference material certificates.
Values associated with performance characteristics of a measurement procedure and the property values stated in documentation are rendered invalid if the minimum sample size is not taken.

basicPropertyValues.val: Lower limit of sample size stipulated in documentation taken for chemical analysis.

comments: A multiplicative matrix effect affects the slope, not the intercept, of a linear calibration curve.
A multiplicative matrix effect can be compensated for by following a measurement procedure with standard addition.
A multiplicative matrix effect may originate from non-analyte components of the measurement standard if these contribute to the signal attributed to the analyte.
The effect is sometimes termed "rotational matrix effect" or "proportional interference".

basicPropertyValues.val: Matrix effect that is proportional to the measured quantity value of the measurand.

comments: A non-certified property value cannot be used as reference in a metrological traceability chain.
A non-certified property value may be included in the reference material certificate or supplied in other form.
In ISO Guide 30, "indicative value", "information value", and "informative value" are admitted terms.

basicPropertyValues.val: Property value that is provided for information only but is not certified by a reference material producer.

comments: In, the term defined is "traceability". However, because of the potential confusion with metrological traceability, it is recommended to use the full term if there is ambiguity.

When considering a product or a service, traceability can relate to: the origin of materials and parts, the processing history, or the distribution and location of the product or service after delivery.

basicPropertyValues.val: Ability to trace the history, application, or location of an object.
Determination of property values obtained in the course of the production of a reference material.

comments: Recovered quantity value ratio may be estimated from the measured change of the quantity value of the component of interest upon the addition of a known amount of substance or mass of the component. The added material containing the component is often termed "spike". See also: blank material Note 5, measurement procedure with standard addition, and spike.
Recovery quantity value ratio is used in procedure validation to evaluate and correct for the measurement procedure bias.

The definition can be symbolized by \(R_{\rm{B}} = Q_{\rm{B,measured}}/Q_{\rm{B,reference}}\), where \(R\) denotes the recovered ratio of the quantity values \(Q\), and \(\ce{B}\) identifies the component.
The quantities involved are rational unitary quantities and of the same kind of quantity, usually either a concentration or content.
The respective measurement procedure must be specified.
The term "recovery" is also used to describe material recovery. Therefore, the term "recovery" should not be used without qualification unless the meaning is clear from the context.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measured quantity value relating a component to a system divided by a reference value.

comments: A condition of measurement is a repeatability condition only with respect to a specified set of repeatability conditions.
A set of measurements under repeatability conditions is often termed "analytical run".

In ISO 3534-2, "same operator" (singular) is stipulated as a repeatability condition. The VIM request of "same operators" (plural) should be understood such that if two or more operators contribute to one measurement, they should be involved in the same way in repeated measurements.
In analytical chemistry, the phrase "under repeatability conditions" refers to the above specified set of conditions.

basicPropertyValues.val: Condition of measurement, out of a set of conditions that includes the same measurement procedure, same operators, same measuring system, same operating conditions, and same location, and replicate measurements on the same or similar objects over a short period of time.

comments: Measurement bias in analytical chemistry may be considered to include run bias, laboratory bias, and measurement procedure bias.

basicPropertyValues.val: Contribution to measurement bias that is attributed to systematic effects on measurement results made in a single analytical run.

comments: Sample pre-treatment includes, for example, mixing, splitting, drying, crushing, stabilization, dissolving, extracting, diluting, precipitating, and derivatizing.

basicPropertyValues.val: Collective noun for all procedures used for conditioning a sample to a defined state which allows subsequent chemical analysis or long-term storage (see material stability).

comments: Sampling often provides a contribution to the measurement uncertainty budget or the examination uncertainty, as applicable.

basicPropertyValues.val: Act of taking or constituting a sample.
Individual portion of material collected by a single operation of a sampling device.

comments: The sampling target may be defined by Regulations (for example, lot size).
The sampling target should be defined prior to designing the sampling plan.

basicPropertyValues.val: Portion of the material, at a particular time, that the sample is intended to represent.

comments: The shelf life is equivalent to the "period of validity" of the reference material certificate and is ended by the "expiry date".

basicPropertyValues.val: Time interval during which a reference material producer warrants the material stability of the reference material.

comments: "Spike" used as a verb is the addition of a spike to a sample.
A spike may be used to estimate the recovered quantity value ratio or compensate for systematic measurement error.
The known quantity value is often a fraction or concentration.
The material can be a reference material or a certified reference material.

basicPropertyValues.val: Material with known quantity values added to an analytical sample.

comments: A systematic effect can be compensated for by a correction.

basicPropertyValues.val: Recognized effect of an influence quantity on a measured quantity value.

comments: In analytical chemistry, testing may be a measurement to obtain a quantity value or an examination, such as identifying a chemical substance (see qualitative analysis).

basicPropertyValues.val: Determination of one or more characteristics of an object of conformity assessment, according to a specified procedure.

comments: In the VIM, the concept is denoted as "quantity expressed by a measurement unit" in the concept diagram Figure A.1 and is referred to as "quantities other than ordinal quantities", for example, in entry 1.21, and as "non-ordinal quantity" in Note 1 to entry 2.41.

basicPropertyValues.val: Quantity with a magnitude expressed as a reference quantity multiplied by a number.

comments: In some fields, the term is "measurement range". In entry 4.7 of VIM, a similar concept termed "measuring interval" is defined.
The lower limit of a working interval should not be confused with the detection limit.
The working interval is bounded by the lower and upper limit of quantification.

basicPropertyValues.val: Set of quantity values over which a measuring instrument or measuring system provides measurement results with acceptable measurement uncertainty under defined conditions.

comments: An acceptance interval is termed an "acceptance zone" in the Eurachem guide on compliance assessment.
Unless otherwise stated in the specification, the acceptance limits belong to the acceptance interval.

basicPropertyValues.val: Interval of permissible measured quantity values.

comments: Permissible measured quantity values are associated with items that conform to specified requirements with at least a predetermined conformance probability and lie within the acceptance interval.

basicPropertyValues.val: Specified upper or lower bound of permissible measured quantity values.

comments: Examples of conformity assessment tasks for which accreditation can be granted are measurement, testing, inspection, provision of proficiency testing schemes, and production of reference materials.

The criteria for determining a laboratory's competence are based on relevant international standards, for example, ISO/IEC 17025, ISO 15189, or ISO 15195, and include adequate quality assurance and quality control procedures, such as qualifications, training and experience of staff, appropriate equipment that is properly calibrated and maintained, use of validated measurement procedures, participation in interlaboratory comparisons, and appropriate sampling practices.

basicPropertyValues.val: Third-party attestation related to a laboratory conveying formal demonstration of its competence to carry out specific conformity assessment tasks.

comments: Selectivity should be qualified by "analytical" if there is potential confusion with selectivity in catalysis or in organic reaction mechanisms.

basicPropertyValues.val: Selectivity of a measuring system in analytical chemistry.

comments: Depending on the role and responsibilities of an assessor, terms such as "lead assessor" and "technical assessor" are often used.
The assessor may work alone or as part of a team and be engaged in a voluntary or paid capacity.
The work of an assessor is often referred to as "assessment" and sometimes as "peer review".

basicPropertyValues.val: Person, assigned by an accreditation body, with relevant professional expertise and experience who can determine the competence of a laboratory.

comments: Options for establishing an assigned value for some types of proficiency testing schemes are detailed in ISO/IEC 17043 and ISO 13528.
The value may be a reference quantity value or a value of a nominal property.

basicPropertyValues.val: Value attributed to a particular property of an item and that serves as an agreed reference for comparison.

comments: An audit can be an internal audit (first party) or an external audit (second party or third party), and it can be a combined audit or a joint audit.

External audits include those generally termed second and third-party audits. Second-party audits are conducted by parties having an interest in the organization, such as customers, or by other persons on their behalf. Third-party audits are conducted by external, independent auditing organizations such as those providing certification/registration of conformity or governmental agencies.

Internal audits, sometimes termed first-party audits, are conducted by, or on behalf of, the organization itself for management review and other internal purposes and can form the basis for an organization's declaration of conformity. Independence can be demonstrated by the freedom from responsibility for the activity being audited.
The fundamental elements of an audit include the determination of the conformity of an object according to a procedure carried out by personnel not being responsible for the object audited.

basicPropertyValues.val: Systematic, independent, and documented process for obtaining objective evidence and evaluating it objectively to determine the extent to which the audit criteria are fulfilled.
Reference material subjected to a process of reference material certification.

comments: A candidate reference material for a given property may already be a reference material for other properties.

basicPropertyValues.val: Material subjected to the procedures necessary to show its fitness for intended use (see fitness for purpose).

comments: Process capability terms in the field of statistics are defined in ISO 3534-2.

basicPropertyValues.val: Ability of an object to realize an output that will fulfil the requirements for that output.

comments: In analytical chemistry, Ishikawa diagrams are used to indicate sources of measurement uncertainty. See Fig. 1. Figure 1: Ishikawa diagram for the titration of a hydrochloric acid solution with sodium hydroxide solution that has been standardized using potassium hydrogen phthalate (KHP). When used for identification of sources of measurement uncertainty, the diagram illustrates how the quantity value of the measurand (\(c_{\ce{HCl}}\)) depends on input quantities in a measurement model (symbols in bold), which in turn depend on other quantities. Symbols have their usual meanings. \(f_{\rm{precision}}\) is a is a factor in the measurement function to account for measurement precision with value 1 and standard measurement uncertainty.

basicPropertyValues.val: Diagram indicating the causes of a specific event or condition.

comments: Certification is applicable to all objects of conformity assessment except for conformity assessment bodies themselves, to which accreditation is applicable.
Certification of a management system is sometimes also termed registration.

basicPropertyValues.val: Third-party attestation related to products, processes, systems, or persons.

comments: Cases in which a reference material producer is required to conduct assessment of commutability are outlined in ISO 15194.
Guidance for assessment of commutability of reference material in laboratory medicine is provided by IFCC.
The material stability of commutable reference materials should be monitored regularly.
The measurement procedures referred to in the definition are the one preceding and the one following the reference material (calibrator) in question in a calibration hierarchy (see ISO 17511).
The reference material in question is usually a calibrator and the other specified materials are usually routine samples.

basicPropertyValues.val: Property of a reference material, demonstrated by the closeness of agreement between the relation among the measurement results for a stated quantity in this material, obtained according to two given measurement procedures, and the relation obtained among the measurement results for other specified materials.

comments: Demonstrated competence is sometimes referred to as "qualification".

basicPropertyValues.val: Ability to apply knowledge and skills to achieve intended results.
Probability that an item fulfils a specified requirement.

comments: "Body" refers to an organization.

The expression "object of conformity assessment" or "object" is used to encompass any particular material, product, installation, process, system, person, or body to which conformity assessment is applied.

The subject field of conformity assessment includes activities, such as testing, calibration, carrying out an audit, inspection, and certification, as well as the accreditation of conformity assessment bodies.

basicPropertyValues.val: Activity to determine whether specified requirements relating to a product, process, system, person, or body are fulfilled.

comments: Control charts are commonly used in the regular monitoring of the performance of a measurement procedure, as part of the laboratory's internal quality control.
Examples of control charts are Shewhart means chart, Shewhart range chart, and cumulative sum control chart.
The control chart operates most effectively when the measure is a process variable which is correlated with an ultimate product or service characteristic.
The particular order is usually based on time or sample number order. Repeated sampling may be avoided where in-situ measurements are applicable.

basicPropertyValues.val: Chart with control limits on which some statistical measure related to a series of samples is plotted in a particular order to steer the process with respect to that measure.

comments: A control limit may be a statistical value or be related to a predetermined target value, calculated, for example, from a target measurement uncertainty.

A typical control chart will consist of a centre line that reflects the level around which the plotted value can be expected to vary. In addition, this control chart will have two lines, called control limits, placed one on each side of the centre line, which define a band within which the value can be expected to lie randomly for a process in a state of statistical control.
A typical response to a value outside a warning limit is to monitor the process and, if this condition is repeated, to stop and investigate.

A value outside an action limit is normally taken as evidence that the process is no longer in statistical control. A typical response to such a value is to stop and investigate. (See process in a state of statistical control).

Control limits on a Shewhart control chart are placed at a distance of ±2σ and ±3σ where σ is the known or estimated standard deviation of the population. This gives approximate probabilities of 0.05 and 0.003, respectively, of finding values outside the control limits. These limits are known as the upper and lower warning limit (UWL and LWL) and upper and lower action limit (UAL and LAL), respectively. See Shewart means chart - Fig. 1.

basicPropertyValues.val: Value defining an intended level of stability for a process.
Person(s) with responsibility for organizing and managing all of the activities involved in the operation of an interlaboratory comparison.

comments: CUSUM charts are particularly sensitive to reveal a small measurement bias.

More suited to spreadsheet analysis, the following quantities are calculated for N measured quantity values \(x_{i} (i=1; …, N)\) \(S_{\rm{hi}}(i) = {\rm{max}}(0,S_{\rm{hi}}(i - 1) + x_{i} - \mu - k)\); \(S_{\rm{hi}}(0) = 0\) \(S_{\rm{lo}}(i) = \rm{max}(0,S_{\rm{lo}}(i - 1) - {x}_{i} + \mu - k)\); \(S_{\rm{lo}}(0) = 0\). \(\mu\) is a suitably chosen target value and \(k\) is a reference quantity value such that only shifts away from the target value greater than \(k\) will add to the cumulative sum. \(k\) is usually taken as half the shift in the process mean that is required to be detected divided by the standard deviation (\(\sigma\)) obtained under repeatability conditions of measurement. An out-of-control criterion is when \(S_{\rm{hi}}(i)\) or \(S_{\rm{lo}}(i)\) becomes greater than a limiting value \(h\) (usually \(h = 4\sigma\)). (Note that the reference quantity value \(k\) is not a coverage factor).
The best discrimination of changes in the level is achieved when the reference quantity value is equal to the overall mean value.
The chart can be used for control, diagnostic, or predictive purposes.
The ordinate of each plotted point represents the algebraic sum of the previous ordinate and the most recent deviation from the reference, target, or control value.

When used for process control, it can be interpreted graphically using a mask (for example, V-mask) superimposed on the graph. An out-of-control criterion is when the path of the cumulative sum intersects or touches the boundary of the mask.

basicPropertyValues.val: Control chart where the cumulative sum of deviations of successive measured quantity values from a reference quantity value is plotted to detect shifts in the level of the measurand.

comments: Decision rules in conformity assessment give a prescription for the acceptance or rejection of an item based on the measured quantity value and the associated measurement uncertainty and limit(s) expressed or implied by specified requirements, taking into account the acceptable level of the probability of making a wrong decision. On the basis of the decision rules, an "acceptance interval" and "rejection interval(s)" are determined, such that if the measured quantity value lies in the acceptance interval, the item is declared as conforming and if in the rejection interval, it is declared as non-conforming.

basicPropertyValues.val: Documented rule that describes how measurement uncertainty will be accounted for with regard to accepting or rejecting an item, given a specified requirement and a measured quantity value.
Ability of a product, process, or service to serve a defined purpose under specific conditions.

comments: A GLP approval should not be confused with accreditation of a laboratory.
GLP is generally associated with the guidelines laid down by the Organization for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD). The use of the term GLP outside these guidelines is not recommended.

basicPropertyValues.val: Quality system concerned with the organizational process, and conditions under which non-clinical health and environmental safety studies are planned, performed, monitored, recorded, archived, and reported.

Combination of manufacturing and quality procedures aimed at ensuring that products are consistently manufactured to their specified requirements and to avoid contamination of the product by internal or external sources.

comments: A guard band is used to restrict or to extend an acceptance interval to reduce the probability of an unwanted decision on conformance due to the measurement uncertainty of the actual measurement. The width of a guard band is scaled with the measurement uncertainty. (See: decision rule in conformity assessment).

If the acceptance limits lie outside the tolerance limits, the decision for conformity of the item is known as guarded rejection. The probability of falsely rejecting a conforming item is reduced. See Fig. 2.

If the acceptance limits lie within the tolerance limits, the decision for conformity of the item is known as guarded acceptance. The probability of falsely accepting a non-conforming item is reduced. This is most often found in chemistry. See Fig. 1.

basicPropertyValues.val: Interval between a tolerance limit and a corresponding acceptance limit. Figure 1: Guarded acceptance. Two-sided acceptance interval created by reducing the tolerance interval on either side by a guard band, thus reducing the probability of falsely accepting a non-conforming item.Figure 2: Guarded rejection. Two-sided acceptance interval created by increasing the tolerance interval on either side by a guard band, thus reducing the probability of falsely rejecting a conforming item.

comments: The shape of the curve is called a trumpet when the relative standard deviation is plotted against the logarithm of the mass fraction as shown in Fig. 1. The reference justifies the mirror curve for negative ordinate values by "… the lines are best regarded as confidence boundaries."

basicPropertyValues.val: Empirical relationship providing a standard deviation under reproducibility conditions of measurement (\(s_{\rm{R,H}}\)) to be expected for typical measurements of the mass fraction (\(w\)) of a component in a material: \(s_{\rm{R,H}} = 0.02 w^{0.8495}\).

comments: In, the "Horwitz ratio" is defined as the ratio of the standard deviation under reproducibility conditions of measurement and standard deviation under repeatability conditions of measurement. This use is discouraged because of the possibility of confusion with the older usage.
The Horwitz ratio is used as a test of the fitness for purpose of methods of chemical analysis.

The experimental measurement precision is better than to be expected from the Horwitz equation if the Horwitz ratio is less than 1 and poorer if greater than 1. In practice, ratios between 0.5 and 2.0 are acceptable.

basicPropertyValues.val: Standard deviation of a mass fraction of a component under reproducibility conditions of measurement divided by the corresponding standard deviation calculated from the Horwitz equation. Figure 1: Horwitz curve (trumpet, horn). Expected relative standard deviation under reproducibility conditions of measurement, \(\pm s_{\rm{R,H}}/w\) plotted against logarithm of mass fraction, \(w\).

comments: The preparation, characterization, and use of in-house reference materials for quality control purposes are described in ISO Guide 80.
Various terms are used to distinguish among reference materials intended for different uses and with assigned values established applying different procedures.

basicPropertyValues.val: Reference material produced and used by an analytical laboratory.

comments: If the result of an inspection shows conformity, it can be used for purposes of verification.
Inspection of processes can include personnel, facilities, technology, or methodology.
Inspection procedures or schemes can restrict inspection to examination only.
The result of an inspection can show conformity or non-conformity or a degree of conformity, where conformity is defined as fulfilment of a requirement.

basicPropertyValues.val: Examination of a product, process, service, or installation or their design and determination of conformity with specific requirements or on the basis of professional judgment, with general requirements.

comments: Accredited laboratories and laboratories seeking accreditation are expected to participate in interlaboratory comparisons, for example, proficiency testing schemes, where available and appropriate.

Determination of performance characteristics of a measurement procedure as part of procedure validation or characterization of a candidate reference material can be done by means of an interlaboratory comparison. (See method performance study and material characterization study.)

In some circumstances, one of the laboratories involved in an interlaboratory comparison may be the laboratory that provides the assigned value for the item. The assignment enables the determination of the metrological equivalence of measurement results of the participants but does not, by itself, establish metrological traceability.

Interlaboratory comparison is a generic term, and the purpose and detailed objectives of an interlaboratory comparison must be specified. Some types of interlaboratory comparisons have special names, for example, proficiency testing scheme and key comparison.

Interlaboratory comparisons are organized at all metrological levels and have the following steps in common. a) A coordinator of an interlaboratory comparison plans the interlaboratory comparison; b) One or more items are sourced by the coordinator, assessed as appropriate, and distributed to the participants in an interlaboratory comparison with instructions; c) The participants conduct measurements, tests, examinations, or other work on the item(s) and report the results back to the coordinator; d) The coordinator evaluates the results and provides feedback to the participants; and e) The coordinator and/or the participants act on the results.

Key comparisons and supplementary comparisons are organized by the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) in support of the International Committee for Weights and Measures (CIPM) Mutual Recognition Arrangement (MRA) in which National Metrology Institutes demonstrate the international equivalence of their measurement standards and the calibration certificates and measurement certificates they issue.

The minimum number of laboratories participating in an interlaboratory comparison will depend on the metrological properties of the measurement procedures used, for example, measurement precision and analytical selectivity. See, performance characteristics of a measurement procedure.
The use of terms such as "ring test", "round robin", "intercalibration", "intercomparison", "collaborative study", etc. for interlaboratory comparisons is not recommended in formal documents.

basicPropertyValues.val: Organization, performance, and evaluation of measurements or tests on the same or similar items by two or more laboratories in accordance with predetermined conditions.
Quality control within a specified laboratory.
Organization, performance, and evaluation of measurements or tests on the same or similar items within the same laboratory in accordance with predetermined conditions.

comments: In laboratory medicine, the term "Laboratory Information System" is common.
LIMS functionality can include sample registration and tracking (through barcodes, chips, etc.), electronic laboratory notebooks, report generation, quality control, and financial control.
Services include the control of automated analyses and collecting, processing, storing, and managing of data.

basicPropertyValues.val: Information system which can provide services to one or more measuring systems.

comments: A material characterization study often utilizes selected (routine or reference) laboratories to measure quantity values of a candidate reference material by measurement procedure(s) judged most likely to provide the smallest associated measurement uncertainty.

Although proficiency testing is not primarily intended as a material characterization study, reference materials are sometimes certified on the basis of results from a proficiency testing scheme after appropriate quality assurance procedures.

basicPropertyValues.val: Intralaboratory comparison or interlaboratory comparison with the aim of assigning a reference quantity value to a quantity with stated measurement uncertainty or value to a reference nominal property value with stated examination uncertainty.

comments: A chemical substance dissolved in a pure solvent is not a matrix reference material.
Matrix reference materials are intended to be used in conjunction with the chemical analysis of real samples of the same or a similar matrix.
Matrix reference materials may also be prepared by a spike of the component(s) of interest into an existing material.
Matrix reference materials may be obtained directly from biological, environmental, or industrial sources.

basicPropertyValues.val: Reference material that is characteristic of a real sample.

comments: A comparison of the measurement uncertainty in the measurement result obtained by one laboratory to that of the measurement result obtained by another laboratory for the same quantity in the same material compares their respective measurement capabilities.

basicPropertyValues.val: Ability to measure a quantity in a specified interval of quantity values, embodied in a specified material, as demonstrated by measurement uncertainty.
Quality control material with or without reference quantity value used in quality control to assess measurement precision.
Quality control material with reference quantity value used in quality control to estimate a systematic measurement error.

comments: Details regarding organizing and conducting the study, for example, type of samples and number of measurements, are specified in a validation plan or in a protocol for interlaboratory comparison.
The general term "collaborative study" should not be used for an interlaboratory method performance study.
The study is normally conducted in the frame of procedure validation or procedure verification.

basicPropertyValues.val: Intra- or interlaboratory study of one or more performance characteristics of a measurement procedure.

comments: In formal documents, the term "body" is often used to denote an organization, for example, "accreditation body", "certification body", "inspection body", "legislative body", and "regulatory body".

The concept of "organization" includes, but is not limited to, sole-trader, company, corporation, firm, enterprise, authority, partnership, association, charity, or institution, or part or combination thereof, whether incorporated or not, public or private.

basicPropertyValues.val: Person or group of people that has its own functions with responsibilities, authorities, and relationships to achieve its objectives.

comments: Decision rules may include those relating to measured quantity values inside and outside of control limits in a control chart. They cover runs, trends, cycles, periodicity, concentration of points near the centre line or control limits, unusual spread of points within control limits (large or small dispersion), and relationships among values within subgroups.
Examples of decision rules and guidelines for the daily interpretation of a control chart are provided by Nordtest.

basicPropertyValues.val: Set of decision rules for identifying the presence of special causes.
Laboratory, organization, or person that receives test items and submits results for review by the coordinator of an interlaboratory comparison.

nodes.lbl: performance characteristic of a measurement procedure

comments: Measurement uncertainty is not a performance characteristic of a particular measurement procedure but a property of the measurement result obtained using that measurement procedure.

Performance characteristics that may be considered in procedure validation are analytical selectivity, sensitivity of a measuring system, working interval, ruggedness of a measurement procedure, linearity of a measuring system, linearity of calibration, critical value, limit of detection, limit of quantification, measurement trueness, and measurement precision.

synonyms.val: performance characteristic of a measurement method

basicPropertyValues.val: Aspect of a measurement procedure that may be quantitatively investigated and assessed as part of procedure validation.

comments: Names and defining equations of frequently used performance scores are listed in Table 1. Their definitions and interpretations are given in ISO/IEC 17043 and ISO 13528.

The purpose of a performance score is to express the deviation of the reported value from the assigned value in a proficiency testing scheme in a manner that allows comparison with performance criteria.

basicPropertyValues.val: Statistic, derived from a result reported by a participant in a proficiency testing scheme, used in interpretation of participant performance and to allow comparison with defined objectives.

comments: ISO 3534-2 defines three kinds of precision limit: repeatability limit (\(r\)), intermediate precision limit, and reproducibility limit (\(R\)) obtained under repeatability conditions of measurement, intermediate precision conditions of measurement, and reproducibility conditions of measurement, respectively. The recommended probability is \(\pu{95\%}\).
Precision limit at approximately \(\pu{95\%}\) is estimated by multiplying the standard deviation obtained under the specified conditions of measurement by \(2\sqrt{2}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: Quantity value, less than or equal to what the absolute difference between two measured quantity values obtained under specified conditions of measurement is expected to be with a given probability.

comments: In ISO/IEC 17025, the term "method" is used as a synonym for measurement procedure.
Inherent in procedure validation is the need to evaluate performance characteristics of a measurement procedure.
Procedure validation is either done in a single laboratory or in the framework of an interlaboratory comparison.
The corresponding term in ISO 15189 is "validation of examination procedures".

basicPropertyValues.val: Process of defining an analytical requirement and confirming that the procedure under consideration has capabilities consistent with that requirement.

comments: A laboratory that implements a procedure described in, for example, an international standard or in a manufacturer"s documentation needs to verify that the procedure fulfils the specified requirements.
In ISO/IEC 17025, the term "method" is used as a synonym for measurement procedure.
The corresponding term in ISO 15189 is "verification of examination procedures".

basicPropertyValues.val: Confirmation, through the provision of objective evidence, that the procedure fulfils specified requirements.

nodes.lbl: process in a state of statistical control

comments: A control chart can be used to monitor a process and to determine whether the process is, or is not, in a state of statistical control. See out-of-control criteria and control limit.
The random variation is considered to follow a Gaussian distribution and is characterized by its variance (standard deviation)
This state does not imply that the random variation is large or small, within or outside of specification, but rather that the variation is predictable using statistical techniques.

basicPropertyValues.val: Process subject only to random causes.
Sample, product, artefact, reference material, piece of equipment, measurement standard, data set, or other information used for proficiency testing.

comments: Participation in proficiency testing schemes is not a substitute for internal quality control measures or vice versa.
Proficiency testing is achieved by the distribution of proficiency test items for unsupervised measurement or examination by the participants.
Some proficiency testing providers in the laboratory medicine area use the term "external quality assessment (EQA)" for their proficiency testing schemes or for their broader programmes, or both.
The evaluation of quantitative results of a participant in a proficiency testing scheme may be given as a \(z\) score, \(z'\) score, \(\zeta\) score, or \(E_{\rm{n}}\) score (see performance score).

The term "proficiency testing" includes, but is not limited to, a) quantitative scheme—where the objective is to quantify one or more measurands of the proficiency test item; b) qualitative scheme—where the objective is to identify or describe one or more characteristics of the proficiency test item; c) sequential scheme—where one or more proficiency test items are distributed sequentially for testing or measurement and results returned to the proficiency testing provider at intervals; d) simultaneous scheme—where proficiency test items are distributed for concurrent testing or measurement within a defined time period; e) single occasion exercise—where proficiency test items are provided on a single occasion; f) continuous scheme—where proficiency test items are provided at regular intervals; g) sampling—where samples are taken for subsequent chemical analysis; and h) data transformation and interpretation—where sets of data or other information are furnished
						and the information is processed to provide an interpretation (or other outcome).

basicPropertyValues.val: Evaluation of the performance of a participant in an interlaboratory comparison against pre-established criteria.
Organization which takes responsibility for all tasks in the development and operation of a proficiency testing scheme.
Single complete sequence from distribution of proficiency test items to reporting of the evaluation results to the participants.

comments: A proficiency testing scheme might cover a particular type or number of tests, measurements, calibrations or inspections on proficiency test items.
The use of terms such as "ring test", "round robin", "intercalibration", "intercomparison", "collaborative study", etc. for proficiency testing schemes is not recommended in formal documents.

basicPropertyValues.val: Proficiency testing designed and operated in one or more proficiency testing rounds for a specified area of testing, measurement, calibration, or inspection.
Detailed set of instructions describing the objectives, design, conduct, and reporting of an interlaboratory comparison.

comments: "Inherent", as opposed to "assigned", means existing in the object.
Measurement uncertainty provides a quantitative measure of the quality of a measurement result.
The term "quality" can be used with adjectives such as poor, good, or excellent.

basicPropertyValues.val: Degree to which a set of inherent characteristics of an object fulfils requirements.

comments: Blank materials, analytical samples, reference materials, and certified reference materials can be used as quality control materials.

basicPropertyValues.val: Material used for the purposes of quality control and subjected to the same or part of the same measurement procedure as that used for analytical samples.

comments: The requirements can be related to any aspect such as effectiveness, efficiency, or object traceability.

basicPropertyValues.val: Part of quality management focused on increasing the ability to fulfil requirements for quality.

comments: Quality management can include establishing quality policies and quality objectives.

basicPropertyValues.val: Coordinated activities to direct and control an organization with regard to quality.

comments: A laboratory's structure, roles and responsibilities, planning, operation, practices, rules, and beliefs are also established within the quality management system.

Other common parts of a laboratory's management system are financial management and environmental management. These management systems should not be confused with a laboratory information management system.

basicPropertyValues.val: Part of a set of interrelated or interacting elements of an organization to establish quality policies and quality objectives and processes to achieve those objectives.

comments: Quality manuals can vary in detail and format to suit the size and complexity of an individual organization.

basicPropertyValues.val: Specification for the quality management system of an organization.

comments: In the context of quality management systems, quality objectives are set by the laboratory, consistent with the quality policy, to achieve specific results.
Quality objectives are generally based on the quality policy of the organization.
Quality objectives are generally specified for relevant functions, levels and processes in the organization.

basicPropertyValues.val: Result to be achieved related to quality.

comments: A quality plan is generally one of the results of quality planning.
A quality plan often refers to parts of the quality manual or to procedure documents.
These procedures generally include those referring to quality management processes and to product and service realization processes.

basicPropertyValues.val: Specification of the procedures and associated resources to be applied when and by whom to a specific object.

comments: Establishing quality plans can be part of quality planning.

basicPropertyValues.val: Part of quality management focused on setting quality objectives and specifying necessary operational processes and related resources to achieve the quality objectives.

comments: Generally, the quality policy is consistent with the overall policy of the laboratory, can be aligned with the laboratory's vision and mission, and provides a framework for the setting of quality objectives.

basicPropertyValues.val: Intentions and direction of a laboratory as formally expressed by its top management related to quality.

comments: In laboratory medicine, a reference measurement laboratory is defined in ISO 15195.
The term "reference laboratory" may have other connotations in a national context.

basicPropertyValues.val: Laboratory that applies a reference measurement procedure, a reference examination procedure, or performs a calibration.

comments: A reference material certificate is usually valid for a stated period of time ("period of validity" or as described by its "expiry date"), which defines the shelf life of the certified reference material.
Documents containing the information described above may not, for legal or other (non-technical) reasons, be termed "certificate" (compare Note 1 to certified reference material).
ISO Guide 31 is the guidance document to the required and recommended content of a reference material certificate.
In this definition, "traceability" covers both metrological traceability of a measurement result and examination traceability, but not object traceability.

basicPropertyValues.val: Document, issued by a reference material producer, containing the essential information for the use of a certified reference material and confirming that the necessary procedures have been carried out to ensure the validity and traceability of the stated property values.

comments: Properties of a material include qualitative properties such as identities of chemical substances and quantitative properties such as mass concentration.
Reference material certification is a "first-party attestation" in accordance with the definition of the term "declaration".
The outcome of the process is a reference material certificate.
The process is the responsibility of the reference material producer.

basicPropertyValues.val: Process that formally establishes the certified property value(s) of a candidate certified reference material.

comments: The information may refer to, for example, the preparation of the reference material, measurement procedures, factors affecting measurement accuracy, statistical treatment of measurement results, and the way in which metrological traceability was established.

basicPropertyValues.val: Document giving detailed information, in addition to that contained in a reference material certificate.

comments: "Body" refers to an organization.
ISO 17034 provides the general requirements for the competence of reference material producers.
The relevant guidance documents are the ISO Guides 31 and 35.

basicPropertyValues.val: Technically competent body that produces a reference material compliant with the appropriate guidance documents and issues the reference material documentation.

comments: Non-permissible measured quantity values are associated with items that do not conform to specified requirements and lie outside the acceptance interval.

basicPropertyValues.val: Interval of non-permissible measured quantity values.

comments: "Generally implied" means that it is custom or common practice for the organization and interested parties that the need or expectation under consideration is implied.
A specified requirement is one that is stated, for example, in documented information.

basicPropertyValues.val: Need or expectation that is stated, generally implied or obligatory.

comments: A measurement procedure, the performance of which remains unaffected by minor changes in operating conditions, is usually said to be "rugged" or "robust".
Ruggedness is normally investigated as a part of procedure development and may be part of procedure validation.
The outcome of a ruggedness test provides objective evidence of the applicability of the measurement procedure during normal usage.

basicPropertyValues.val: Ability of a measurement procedure to maintain acceptable performance under minor changes in operating conditions.

comments: Sensitivity of a measuring system can be obtained from the slope of the calibration curve.
Sensitivity of a measuring system can depend on the value of the quantity being measured.
Sensitivity of a measuring system should not be confused with diagnostic sensitivity in laboratory medicine.
Sensitivity of a measuring system should not be confused with limit of detection or limit of quantification.
The change considered in a value of a quantity being measured must be large compared with the resolution.

basicPropertyValues.val: Quotient of the change in an indication of a measuring system and the corresponding change in a quantity being measured.
Control chart with Shewhart control limits intended primarily to distinguish between the variation in the plotted measure due to random causes and that due to special causes.
Control limit determined statistically from the variation of the process due to random causes alone.

comments: Nordtest terms a control chart with measured quantity values scaled by the mean or target value an "X-chart". ISO uses the term "X-control chart" for a control chart which plots single values.

basicPropertyValues.val: Shewhart control chart in which the means of measured quantity values are plotted against time. Figure 1: Shewhart means chart of the means of duplicate analyses of a quality control material, twice per day (d) over 20 days. Each point is the mean of the day’s four results (\(n = 4\)). Upper and lower warning limits (UWL and LWL) are at \(\bar{x} \pm 2s/\sqrt{n}\), where \(\bar{x}\) is the process mean, \(s\) is the standard deviation under repeatability conditions of measurement, and upper and lower action limits (UAL and LAL) are at \(\bar{x} \pm 3s/\sqrt{n}\). A simulated measurement bias of one standard deviation is applied after day 10.

comments: Nordtest advises that for Shewhart range charts, the best samples to be used are test samples selected from among the samples to be analysed in that analytical run.
The range is the greatest measured quantity value minus the least measured quantity value.
Warning and action limits are given in tables (for example) as a function of the number of measured quantity values (\(n\)) taken to obtain the range and of the expected average range.

basicPropertyValues.val: Shewhart control chart in which the ranges of measured quantity values are plotted against time.
Need or expectation that is stated.

comments: Not all proficiency testing schemes evaluate proficiency based on the dispersion of results.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measure of dispersion used in the evaluation of results of proficiency testing.

comments: Laboratory activities for which standard operating procedures are issued include sampling, measurement, testing, and examination.

basicPropertyValues.val: Authorized, documented procedure or set of procedures with detailed instructions for specified activities.

comments: Although statistical process control originally was concerned primarily with manufactured goods, it is also equally applicable to processes producing services, for example, a measurement procedure.

basicPropertyValues.val: Activities focused on the use of statistical techniques to reduce variation, increase knowledge about the process, and steer the process in the desired way.

comments: Setting and using target uncertainty is described in.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement uncertainty specified as an upper limit and decided on the basis of the intended use of measurement results.

comments: Tolerance should not be confused with measurement uncertainty.

basicPropertyValues.val: Difference between upper and lower tolerance limits.

comments: A permissible quantity value of a specified quantity is required of an item fulfilling a specified requirement.
Permissible quantity values must not be confused with permissible measured quantity value of an acceptance interval.
The term "tolerance interval" as used in conformity assessment has a different meaning from the same term as it is used in statistics.
Unless otherwise stated in a specified requirement, the tolerance limits belong to the tolerance interval.

basicPropertyValues.val: Specified upper or lower bound of permissible quantity values of a property.
Organization-wide efforts to install a permanent climate in which an organization continuously improves its ability to deliver high-quality products and services to customers.

comments: In the VIM, "validation" is defined as "verification, where the specified requirements are adequate for an intended use".
The objective evidence needed for a validation is the result of a test or other form of determination such as performing alternative calculations or reviewing documents.
The term "validated" is used to designate the corresponding status.
The use conditions for validation can be real or simulated.

basicPropertyValues.val: Confirmation, through the provision of objective evidence, that the requirements for a specific intended use or application have been fulfilled.

comments: In the VIM, "verification" is defined as "provision of objective evidence that a given item fulfils specified requirements".
The activities carried out for verification are sometimes termed "qualification process".
The objective evidence needed for verification can be the result of an inspection or of other forms of determination such as performing alternative calculations or reviewing documents.
The term "verified" is used to designate the corresponding status.

basicPropertyValues.val: Confirmation, through the provision of objective evidence, that specified requirements have been fulfilled.

comments: The Youden plot is a simple but effective method for comparing both within-laboratory variability and between-laboratory variability.
The coordinates of each point may be the measured quantity values themselves or any transformation thereof such as a performance score, for example, a \(z\) score (see Fig. 1).

basicPropertyValues.val: Graphical technique for evaluating an interlaboratory comparison when each participant has made two measurements on the same sample or one measurement on each of two different samples.Figure 1: Youden plot of the \(z\) scores of samples #9 and #10 of Round 5 of U39 of the proficiency testing program held by the RCPA Australia for the analysis of creatinine in urine by 218 laboratories. (Reproduced with permission).

comments: Often used as a synonym for activated complex or transition state, but not restricted to transition-state theory.
This is distinct from an energized molecule, often characterized by the superscript \(^{\ast}\), in which excitation energy is dispersed among internal degrees of freedom.
This is not a complex according to the definition in this Glossary.

basicPropertyValues.val: In theories of unimolecular reactions an energized chemical species, often characterized by the superscript \(^{\ddagger}\), where the excitation is specific and the molecule is poised for reaction.

comments: The distinction between ambi (Latin: both) and amphi (Greek: both) and the application to hydrophilic and lipophilic or to nucleophilic and electrophilic is arbitrary.

basicPropertyValues.val: 1) Designation applied to the carbon to which a functional group is attached. 2) In carbohydrate nomenclature, a stereochemical designation of the configuration at the anomeric carbon. 3) Parameter in a Brønsted relation expressing the sensitivity of the rate of protonation to acidity. 4) Parameter in Leffler’s relation expressing the sensitivity of changes in Gibbs activation energy to changes in overall Gibbs energy for an elementary reaction.
Feature of a ligand with two potential binding sites.

Feature on a potential-energy surface whereby a minimum-energy reaction path (MERP) emanating from a saddle point (corresponding to a transition structure) splits in two and leads to alternative products without intervening minima or secondary barriers to overcome. A bifurcation arises when the curvature of the surface in a direction perpendicular to the MERP becomes zero and then negative; it implies the existence of a lower-energy transition structure with a transition vector orthogonal to the original MERP.

comments: Although \({\rm{D}}H^{\circ}\) is commonly used, \(\Delta_{\rm{diss}} H^{\circ}\) is more consistent with the notation for other thermodynamic quantities.

basicPropertyValues.val: Standard molar enthalpy required to break a given bond of some specific molecular entity by homolysis.

comments: More commonly, tabulated mean bond energies (which are really enthalpies) are values of bond enthalpies averaged over a number of selected chemical species containing that type of bond, such as \(\pu{414 kJ mol-1}\) for \(\ce{C-H}\) bonds in a group of \(\ce{R3CH}\) (\(\ce{R = H}\), alkyl).

basicPropertyValues.val: Average value of the gas-phase bond-dissociation enthalpies (usually at a temperature of \(\pu{298 K}\)) for all bonds of the same type within the same chemical species.

comments: This feature arises because the potential-energy surface, which describes how the energy of the molecule depends on geometry, shows two (or more) minima that are not merely symmetry-related.

basicPropertyValues.val: Two (or more) molecules with the same spin multiplicity but with different lengths for one or more bonds.

comments: \(\beta_{\rm{nuc}}\) and \(\beta_{\lg}\) are used to correlate nucleophilic reactivity and leaving-group ability, respectively.

basicPropertyValues.val: Parameter in a Brønsted relation expressing the sensitivity of the rate of deprotonation to basicity.
Transformation of the general type \[\ce{XABY -> A=B + XY (or X + Y, or X^{+} + Y^{-})}\] where the central atoms \(\ce{A}\) and \(\ce{B}\) are commonly, but not necessarily, carbon.
Quantitative measure of solvent polarity, based on the solvent’s hydrogen-bond-donor ability, hydrogen-bond-acceptor ability, polarizability, and dipolarity.

comments: A catalytic antibody acts by binding its antigen and catalyzing a chemical reaction that converts the antigen into desired products. Despite the existence of natural catalytic antibodies, most of them were specifically designed to catalyze desired chemical reactions.

Catalytic antibodies are produced through immunization against a transition-state analogue for the reaction of interest. The resulting antibodies bind strongly and specifically the transition-state analogue, so that they become catalysts for the desired reaction.
The concept of catalytic antibodies and the strategy for obtaining them were advanced by W. P. Jencks. The first catalytic antibodies were finally produced in 1986.

basicPropertyValues.val: Sequence of reaction steps in the form of a loop. One step is binding of a reactant to the active catalyst (sometimes formed from a precatalyst), and another step is the release of product and regeneration of the catalyst.
Noncovalent attractive force between a positive ion (metal cation, protonated Brønsted base, etc.) and a \(\ce{\uppi\ electron}\) system.
Structural characteristic rendering a molecule chiral.
Attraction between molecules through noncovalent interactions that exhibit complementarity only between partners with specific chirality.

comments: Because the atomic orbitals that interchange roles are orthogonal, such a reaction does not proceed through a fully conjugated transition state and is thus not a pericyclic reaction. It is therefore not governed by the rules that express orbital symmetry restrictions applicable to pericyclic reactions.

basicPropertyValues.val: Feature of a concerted transformation in which the primary changes in bonding occur within a cyclic array of atoms but in which two nonbonding atomic orbitals on an atom interchange roles with two bonding orbitals.

comments: This term is sometimes also called a line formula, because it can be written on a single line, but the line formula explicitly shows all bonds.

basicPropertyValues.val: Linear representation of the structure of a molecular entity in which bonds are omitted.

comments: Single-headed curly arrows are used to depict the flow of unpaired electrons.
The tail of the curly arrow shows where an electron pair originates, and the head of the curly arrow shows where the electron pair goes.

basicPropertyValues.val: Symbols for depicting the flow of electrons in a chemical reaction or to generate additional resonance forms.

comments: The name comes from the Greek δενδρον (dendron), which translates to "tree". Synonymous terms include arborols and cascade molecules.

basicPropertyValues.val: Large molecule constructed from a central core with repetitive branching and multiple functional groups at the periphery.

Method for analyzing activation energy as the sum of the energies to distort the reactants into the geometries they have in transition states plus the energy of interaction between the two distorted reactants.

comments: Donicity is often used as a measure of a solvent’s basicity.

basicPropertyValues.val: Quantitative experimental measure of the Lewis basicity of a molecule \(\ce{B}\), expressed as the negative enthalpy of the formation of the 1:1 complex \(\ce{B.SbCl5}\).

comments: Customarily, this does not apply to samples where the composition of the sample, and thus its NMR spectrum, changes with time, but rather to samples at equilibrium, without any net reaction. The occurrence of chemical reactions is manifested by features of the NMR line-shape or by magnetization transfer.

basicPropertyValues.val: NMR spectroscopy of samples undergoing chemical reactions.

comments: The electron movement may be intramolecular or intermolecular.
When a single electron is transferred, a single-headed curly arrow or "fish-hook" is used, but the electron movement in the opposite direction is redundant and sometimes omitted.
