PFG techniques are used in magnetic resonance imaging, spatially-selective NMR, and diffusion ordered NMR spectroscopy (DOSY).
The net result of the pulse is that spins are dispersed in the transverse plane (defocussed) and produce zero net magnetization.

basicPropertyValues.val: Short, timed pulse in nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy that momentarily destroys the magnetic field homogeneity within the sample through a spatial-dependent field intensity.

nodes.lbl: pure shift yielded by chirp excitation

comments: The effect is achieved through the concatenation of partial free induction decays generated with a series of swept adiabatic pulses.

basicPropertyValues.val: Nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy experiment generating homonuclear spin-spin decoupled spectra.

Collection of time domain nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy data on both the \(x\) and \(y\ (\rm{g})\) axes of the rotating frame of reference to allow discrimination of positive and negative frequencies.
Nuclide with spin quantum number \(I \gt ½\) and a non-spherical distribution of charge in the nucleus giving rise to a nuclear electric quadrupole moment (\(eQ\)).
Relaxation mechanism in nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy arising from intramolecular quadrupolar interactions with electric field gradients.

comments: Radiation damping can also produce other effects including changes to amplitude and phase of adjacent peaks.

Radiation damping occurs when the rotating transverse magnetization of the sample is intense enough to induce large enough electromotive force in the radiofrequency coil strong enough that it feeds back to the sample. This causes a rotation of magnetization back to the \(+z\) axis and results in line-broadening of the intense peak.

basicPropertyValues.val: Line-broadening effect on intense signals in high field nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy.
In nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, an inductor-capacitor resonant circuit used to set up \(B_{1}\) magnetic inductions in a sample and to detect the signal from the sample.

comments: Usually only the real frequency data is displayed and in simple 1D spectra equates to the NMR signals being absorption mode (in-phase).

basicPropertyValues.val: In nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, one of two equally sized blocks of frequency data \(\pu{90\!^{\circ}}\) out of phase to each other produced by Fourier transformation of the time domain signal.
Paramagnetic species added to a sample in a nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy experiment to promote more rapid spin-lattice relaxation and allow a faster pulse repetition rate.
Time duration between repetitions of a nuclear magnetic resonance pulse sequence including the pulse sequence, acquisition time and relaxation delay.

comments: RDC is typically achieved through partial alignment of molecules in the liquid state through spatially aligned gels or liquids.
RDC is used to provide 3D structural information on molecules.

basicPropertyValues.val: Dipolar coupling, but of a reduced magnitude to that seen in solids, observed in a liquid sample between spins in a molecule where there is incomplete averaging of spatially anisotropic dipolar couplings.

comments: ROESY has the advantage over the NOESY experiment that its response does not go through a null at specific correlation times and is thus preferred for molecules having molecular masses of a few thousand \(\pu{Da}\).

ROESY is similar to the NOESY experiment (see nuclear Overhauser effect spectroscopy) and is useful for determining which signals arise from protons that are close to each other in space even if they are not bonded.

synonyms.val: cross-relaxation appropriate for minimolecules emulated by locked spins (CAMELPSIN)

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement method of nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy yielding through-space correlations via spin-spin relaxation.
Measurement method of nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy allowing recoupling of heteronuclear dipolar coupling under magic angle spinning.

comments: Range of applicable dissociation constants is approximately \(\pu{E-3 M}\) to \(\pu{E-8 M}\). The experiment relies on ligand-signal attenuation through spin diffusion saturation propagating from the macromolecule.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement method of nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy that allows detection of transient binding of small molecule ligands to macromolecular receptors.
Spin decoupling of a specific resonance by selective irradiation.

comments: Selective excitation is usually achieved through the application of long, low power (soft) pulses.

basicPropertyValues.val: Application of a frequency selective radiofrequency pulse(s) to a single resonance or a discrete band of frequencies.
Radiofrequency pulse with a narrow frequency spectral bandwidth (long, low-power pulse) to excite nuclei in a limited chemical shift range (see selective excitation).

nodes.lbl: single crystal nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy

comments: A large crystal is mounted on a 'tenon', which is in turn mounted on a goniometer head. If the orientation of the unit cell is known with respect to the tenon, then it is possible to determine the orientation of the NMR interaction tensors with respect to the molecular frame.

basicPropertyValues.val: Solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy on a single crystal in a similar manner to that used in X-ray diffraction.

comments: SSNMR is characterized by the presence of anisotropic (directionally dependent) interactions. Chemical shift anisotropy (CSA) and internuclear dipolar coupling result in severe line-broadening of the corresponding NMR signals and specific hardware and methods are required to perform SSNMR to mitigate some of these issues including magic angle spinning (MAS).

basicPropertyValues.val: Application of nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy to solids.

In nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy reduction or removal of large, unwanted resonances from solvents to improve spectrum quality and dynamic range through selective excitation and exploiting differences in relaxation times between solvent and analyte signals.
Frequency range that describes the width of the spectrum window of a specific nucleus in nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy.

comments: In nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, only nuclei with spin \(I \gt 0\) are observable.
Nuclei with a spin of \(½\) generate the simplest nuclear magnetic resonance spectra and are thus the most commonly studied.
The magnitude of nuclear spin is \((h/2\pi)\sqrt{I(I + 1)}\) where \(I\) is the spin quantum number and \(h\) is the Planck constant.
The spin of a nucleus is dependent on the numbers and alignments of the spins of its individual protons and neutrons.

basicPropertyValues.val: Intrinsic angular momentum of a nucleus (or other sub-atomic particle).
Irradiation of a nucleus in nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy to prevent spin-spin coupling.

comments: SE is typically used within a pulse sequence to refocus chemical shift by pulses \(\pu{90\!^{\circ}}\), \(T_{\rm{E}}/2\), \(\pu{180\!^{\circ}}\), \(T_{\rm{E}}/2\).

The simplest form of the spin-echo pulse sequence consists of \(\pu{90\!^{\circ}}\ \rm{pulse}\), a \(\pu{180\!^{\circ}}\ \rm{pulse}\), and then an echo. The time between the middle of the first RF pulse and the peak of the spin echo is called the echo time (\(T_{\rm{E}}\)).

basicPropertyValues.val: Refocusing of spin magnetization usually by two consecutive radiofrequency pulses.
Group of magnetic nuclei that interact amongst themselves through spin-spin coupling but do not interact with any nuclei outside the spin system.

comments: \(T_{1}\) dictates the time required between individual NMR scans to ensure the system has returned to equilibrium.

basicPropertyValues.val: Mechanism in nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy by which the component of the magnetization vector along the direction of the static magnetic induction reaches thermodynamic equilibrium with its surroundings through loss of energy of the excited nuclear spins to the surrounding molecular lattice. The resultant exponential decay of signal is characterized by the spin-lattice relaxation time \(T_{1}\) (reciprocal of the rate constant of this mechanism).
Reciprocal of the rate constant of longitudinal relaxation.

comments: In solid state nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy this occurs if the sample is spun at a rate less than the magnitude of the anisotropic interaction.

basicPropertyValues.val: Satellite peaks in a nuclear magnetic resonance spectrum symetrically spaced either side of a main peak at a frequency offset related to the rate of spinning of the sample.

comments: The resultant exponential decay of signal is characterized by the spin-spin relaxation time \(T_{2}\) (reciprocal of the rate constant of this mechanism).

basicPropertyValues.val: Loss of magnetization in the \(xy\) plane (in the absence of \(\boldsymbol{B_{0}}\) inhomogeneities) through the interchange of energy between nuclear spins resulting in some precessing faster than the Larmor angular frequency and some slower.
Reciprocal of the rate constant of spin-spin relaxation.

comments: Static magnetic induction is related to the magnetic field \(\boldsymbol{H}\) through the equation \(\boldsymbol{B} = \mu \boldsymbol{H}\) where \(\mu\) is the permeability of the material.
The value of \(\boldsymbol{B_{0}}\) is expressed in Tesla or as the nominal proton precession frequency (e.g., \(\pu{14 T}\) or \(\pu{600 MHz}\)).

basicPropertyValues.val: Flux density of the magnetic field of a nuclear magnetic resonance spectrometer about whose direction the nuclear magnetic moment precesses.

Method of removing artefacts from a two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance spectrum that are symmetrical about the diagonal (e.g., HH COSY) or the \(\rm{f}1\) axis (e.g., tilted J-resolved spectra). Values equidistant from midline are compared and replaced the lower (or average) value of the two.
Time domain arising from the regular increments of the delay period in two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy.
Time domain in two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy arising from direct free induction decay detection.
Streaks of spurious artefact signals in a two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance spectrum parallel to the \(\rm{f}1\) axis at the \(\rm{f}2\) of a strong resonance.

comments: A 3-D NMR experiment may be constructed from a 2-D NMR experiment by inserting an additional indirect evolution time and a second mixing period between the first mixing period and the direct data acquisition.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement method of nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy in which data are collected in three time domains.
Condition in nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy where the independent variable of all functions is time.

nodes.lbl: time domain nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement method of nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy run at low magnetic field strengths where data analysis is performed directly on the free induction decay, often through the extraction of relaxation time constants

comments: TOCSY uses a spin lock to allow propagation of magnetization through scalar couplings.

basicPropertyValues.val: Two-dimensional nuclear magnetic resonance homonuclear correlation experiment, which creates correlations between all protons within a given spin system, not just between geminal or vicinal protons as in COSY.
Technique to suppress spinning sidebands in solid-state nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy with cross polarization in magic angle spinning experiments.

comments: TROSY relies on the cancellation of the dipolar coupling and chemical shift anisotropy (CSA) components of the transverse relaxation (see spin-spin relaxation).

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement method of nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, usually in protein NMR, that improves peak sharpness for molecules having a molecular mass of greater than \(\pu{100 kDa}\).

comments: For proteins the three nuclei are usually \(\ce{^{1}H}\) hydrogen, \(\ce{^{13}C}\) carbon, and \(\ce{^{15}N}\) nitrogen, which requires suitable labelling of the sample.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement method of nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy using three NMR-active nuclei.

comments: The resulting data matrix is subjected to two successive Fourier transforms to produce a spectrum with two frequency axes, usually either chemical shift/chemical shift (correlation spectroscopy) or chemical shift/J-coupling (see J-resolved spectroscopy).

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement method of nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy in which data are collected in two time domains: acquisition of the free induction decay (\(t_{2}\)) and a successively incremented delay (\(t_{1}\)).

nodes.lbl: wideband, alternating-phase, low-power technique for residual splitting

comments: WALTZ is commonly used for proton decoupling during the acquisition of \(\ce{^{13}C}\) spectra.

basicPropertyValues.val: Cluster of pulses applied repeatedly for heteronuclear decoupling.
Energy levels of a nucleus arising from the interaction of its magnetic dipole with an external magnetic field.

Measurement method of nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy in which nuclear magnetic resonance spectra are acquired in an environment carefully screened from magnetic fields, including from the Earth’s field allowing the direct detection of J-spectra in the absence of Zeeman interactions (see Zeeman levels).
Bombardment of a sample surface with ions resulting in the removal of atoms from their lattice sites, and thus an ongoing discharge process that causes continuous ablation of the sample.
Mass of sample removed in laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy divided by the energy delivered by the laser beam.

comments: Ablation rate is usually expressed in \(\pu{nm s-1}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: Depth of sample layer removed in the glow discharge process per unit time.
Minimum fluence required to achieve ablation of the sample.
Increase in signal equilibration time or in wash out time caused by a modification in inorganic acid concentration.

comments: An inert diluent is non-reactive, an auxiliary gas is reactive.

basicPropertyValues.val: Gases added to a combustion mixture.

comments: These phenomena include solvent evaporation, droplet coalescence or coagulation, inertial droplet losses, gravitational settling and turbulence losses.

basicPropertyValues.val: Processes occurring inside the spray chamber or desolvation system responsible for the modification of the primary aerosol to finally yield the tertiary aerosol.
Mass of analyte reaching the plasma per unit time.

Measurement method of atomic spectroscopy for measuring the amount of a chemical element based on the measurement of the absorption of characteristic electromagnetic radiation by atoms in the vapour phase.

Measurement method of atomic spectroscopy for measuring the amount of a chemical element based on the measurement of the intensity of characteristic electromagnetic radiation emitted by atoms or molecules.
Atomizer intended to convert free atoms to an excited state.

comments: The wavelengths of the absorbed and re-emitted radiation may be identical (atomic resonance fluorescence spectroscopy) or different.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement method of atomic spectroscopy for measuring the amount of a chemical element based on the measurement of the re-emission of characteristic electromagnetic radiation by atoms, following the absorption of radiation in the vapour phase.
Vapour containing free atoms of analyte.
Graph of absorbance against atomization temperature.

comments: Matrix interferences, which originate in the cooler plasma tail, can degrade precision and accuracy.
The large amount of light captured in this method, includes information from the sample of interest plus background, which can be considerable.

basicPropertyValues.val: Inductively-coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer configuration in which the entrance slit is aligned with the main plasma axis.

comments: The continuum emission originates from Bremsstrahlung radiation, which predominates the first part of the plasma life time and decreases with further plasma evolution.

basicPropertyValues.val: Intense continuous background usually observed in laser-induced breakdown spectra.
Concentration of a given element measured at a given wavelength providing the same intensity as the background.

comments: Usually the breakdown-threshold fluence is orders of magnitude higher than the ablation-threshold fluence.

basicPropertyValues.val: Minimum fluence required to achieve measurable emission signals
Plasma generated by a capacitor in presence of a microwave field.

comments: Characteristic lines include resonance and non-resonance lines.

basicPropertyValues.val: Spectral line of an atom used for the measurement of analyte concentration by atomic spectroscopy.

comments: The use of such a source allows for correction of spectral interferences.

basicPropertyValues.val: Source that emits electromagnetic radiation with relatively constant intensity over a broad spectral region.

comments: Depth profile analysis can be accomplished by time resolved measurement of the generated emission signals.
Depth profiling using signal versus time measurement requires knowledge of the ablation rate, which must be known, or has to be calculated, from measurements of suitable materials.

basicPropertyValues.val: Process by which the sample is sputtered 'atomic layer by layer' using suitable conditions.

nodes.lbl: direct current glow discharge optical emission spectroscopy

comments: DC GD-OES is only applicable for electrically conducting samples.

Generated argon ions impact with high energy on to the surface of the cathode, which can thus be ablated in a purely mechanical way (cathodic sputtering) or the cathode can be heated to assist evaporation (thermal volatilization).

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement method using optical emission spectroscopy in which atomization and excitation occur in a glow electric discharge sustained by a direct current electric field.
Conversion of the whole or part of a liquid or solid sample into a physical form sufficiently finely divided to allow it to be atomized (see atomization) upon introduction into the atomizer.

Measurement method of laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy in which reactions are induced by the interaction of the evolved plasma and the remaining part of the laser pulse, or with a following laser pulse provided from a second laser system.
Inductively-coupled plasma spectrometer that allows axial viewing mode or radial viewing mode.

comments: An inductively-coupled plasma is a kind of electric discharge.

basicPropertyValues.val: Transmission of electrical current by a plasma in an applied electric field through a normally non-conducting medium.

comments: SI unit: \(\pu{m-3}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: Number of free electrons in vapour phase per volume unit.
Measurement method of atomic absorption spectroscopy in which the sample is atomized by an electrothermal atomizer.
Technique for sample introduction based on the use of a solid furnace heated at a controlled temperature to vaporize the sample prior to its introduction into an inductively-coupled plasma.
Energy that must be supplied to an atom to transfer it from the ground atomic state to a given ionic excited state.
Spectrometer to make measurements by flame atomic spectroscopy.
Measurement method of atomic spectroscopy that uses a flame to excite atoms.

comments: The flame in general consists of a primary-combustion zone, a secondary-combustion zone and an interconal zone.

basicPropertyValues.val: Continuously flowing mixture of hot gases with a stationary position that derives its heat content from a strongly exothermic, irreversible chemical reaction between a fuel and an oxidant.
Component of a flame atomic spectrometer for creating turbulence in the stream of mist in the spray chamber and removing the largest droplets from this mist by deposition.

comments: The gate delay varies from some hundreds of nanoseconds to several microseconds.
Use of a suitable gate delay allows the high intensity background continuum emission present in the early stages of plasma formation to be removed.

synonyms.val: time delay in laser induced breakdown spectroscopy

basicPropertyValues.val: Time between the application of a laser pulse and the start of detection in laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy.

comments: GD-OES spectrometers mostly use the so called Paschen–Runge mounting, where the entrance slit, the curved grating and different detectors are aligned along the Rowland circle. Alternatively, Echelle spectrometers (see GD-OES spectrometers with simultaneous detection) are used, which use an Echelle grating in combination with a prism for wavelength separation.

basicPropertyValues.val: Spectrometers for glow discharge optical emission spectroscopy that allow simultaneous monitoring of selected spectral ranges or the whole emission spectra.
Fraction of the energy generated being used for creating and maintaining the plasma in an inductively-coupled plasma spectrometer.

comments: Glow discharge allows volatilization as well as excitation of analytes and sample matrices.

basicPropertyValues.val: Component of an atomic emission spectrometer employing a glow electric discharge used in atomic emission spectroscopy for qualitative and quantitative analysis of solid materials.

comments: In atomic emission spectroscopy argon is used as the inert working gas that generates the plasma.
In the prevailing electrical field the produced ions are accelerated towards the cathode, resulting in a continuous bombardment of the sample surface.

basicPropertyValues.val: Electric discharge in gas at low pressure (\(\pu{100}\) to \(\pu{1000 Pa}\)).
Optical emission spectroscopy in which a glow electric discharge excites atoms at the surface of a sample, which is made the cathode of the discharge.

Cathode for a glow electric discharge consisting of a flat sample, which is cooled during the discharge process so that thermal volatilization is suppressed and the sample material is removed by sputtering only.

comments: For this source, sample volatilization takes place mainly by thermal effects.

basicPropertyValues.val: Glow discharge source with a graphite cathode, into which the sample is inserted in the form of drillings, a pressed pellet or a dry solution residue.

comments: It is often referred to as line source, as opposed to a continuum source.

basicPropertyValues.val: Glow discharge source of spectral lines of an atom in which the cathode is made of the desired element.
Power supplied by a generator to the plasma.

Plasma produced by induction by means of a high-frequency (about \(\pu{2500 Hz}\)) electromagnetic field. The region of gas at high temperature and free from the field is taken as the region of observation.

comments: ICP methods are described by their method of detection of ions in the plasma and include inductively-coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy, and inductively-coupled plasma mass spectrometry.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement method of atomic spectroscopy that uses an inductively-coupled plasma to excite and ionize atoms.
Measurement method of atomic spectrometry that uses an inductively-coupled plasma to excite and ionize atoms with measurement of the number and kind of ions in the plasma using mass spectrometry.

Measurement method of atomic spectroscopy that uses an inductively-coupled plasma to excite and ionize atoms with measurement of the number and kind of ions in the plasma from their emission of electromagnetic radiation (see optical emission spectroscopy).

Ability of an inductively-coupled plasma to withstand slight modification in the operating conditions and/or matrix composition with no significant changes in its fundamental characteristics (i.e., temperatures, electron number density) or the analytical figures of merit (i.e., sensitivity, detection limits or signal-to-noise ratio)

Decrease in the inductively-coupled plasma volume normally caused when an organic volatile solution is delivered to it. Organic vapours diffuse towards the outermost area of the plasma and its volume decreases.

comments: In ICP the torch is an open three concentric tubes assembly allowing the introduction of the three gas streams constituting the plasma. The inner tube of the torch can be made of a different material such as alumina and is usually called the injector.

basicPropertyValues.val: Quartz component of an inductively-coupled plasma spectrometer where the plasma is generated and stabilized.
Inductively-coupled plasma volume in inductively-coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy where the analytically-relevant light emission begins to be observed.
Graph of absorbance or intensity plotted as a function of the concentration of an interfering element in an atomic spectroscopy experiment.

comments: Inverse Bremsstrahlung increases the kinetic energy of the electrons, which is important for heating the plasma.

basicPropertyValues.val: Absorption of photon energy by free electrons.
Gas phase containing free ions of analyte.
Removal of material as an aerosol from a surface on irradiation by a laser beam.

Measurement method of atomic spectroscopy that uses a focused laser beam to ablate, atomize and excite atoms from a sample surface with subsequent measurement of the generated electromagnetic radiation.

comments: LIBS spectra cover a wide wavelength range. Commonly, LIBS measurements are taken between the wavelengths of \(\pu{200 nm}\) and \(\pu{1000 nm}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: Emission spectrum generated as a consequence of the decay of the excited states generated in a laser-induced plasma that consists of a continuous background and element-specific atomic or ionic lines and molecular bands.

comments: As well as electrons, laser-induced plasma contains ions, and neutral atoms as well as excited species of the ablated matter. Decay of these excited species generates the light emission analysed in laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy.

basicPropertyValues.val: Local plasma formed by the interaction between a laser beam and a solid sample and initiated by the production of primary electrons by multiphoton ionization and thermionic photoemission mechanisms.

comments: Line-broadening increases the measurement uncertainty of a measurement.

basicPropertyValues.val: Increase in the theoretical width of a spectral line owing to thermal motion of emitting atoms (Doppler effect), to electric field (Stark effect), to self-absorption and to pressure (Lorentz effect).
Graph of the variation of emitted radiation intensity as a function of wavelength (emission line) or the variation of the absorption factor as a function of wavelength (absorption line).

comments: The system is normally composed of a micro-nebulizer and a low inner volume spray chamber.

basicPropertyValues.val: Liquid-sample introduction system to an inductively-coupled plasma spectrometer adapted to work at sample flow rates below \(\pu{100 \upmu L min-1}\).
Number of detector events per atom in the sample.
Resonant cavity that permits focusing a microwave field inside a discharge tube thus giving rise to a standing wave.

comments: The plasma results as a consequence of ionization of a given gas in presence of electrons and a microwave field.

basicPropertyValues.val: Plasma generated in a microwave cavity.
Conversion of a liquid into an aerosol consisting of droplets suspended in a gas stream.

comments: These effects include scattering or absorption effects by solid particles.

basicPropertyValues.val: Electromagnetic radiation, within the bandpass filter used, emitted by, or absorption caused by, atoms, molecules and radicals that are subject to the atomizer by all components, apart from the analyte, that are present there during measurement.

Inductively-coupled plasma volume mainly responsible for emission of analytically-useful light because processes leading to excited species, such as droplet desolvation, element vaporization, atomization (or ionization) and excitation have been completed.

comments: OES is used as the detector in inductively-coupled plasma optical emission spectroscopy, and glow-discharge optical emission spectroscopy.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement principle of atomic emission spectroscopy in which the emitted electromagnetic radiation is in the range of frequencies from the infrared, through visible, to the ultra-violet region.
In atomic spectroscopy, mass of analyte converted into free atoms in the atomizer divided by mass of analyte entering the dispersion device.
Collisional excitation and ionization mechanism of inductively-coupled plasma spectrometry involving analyte atoms and metastable argon atoms.
In atomic spectroscopy, flux of mass of sample divided by the flux of mass of solvent blank, measured under the same conditions, expressed as a percentage.

comments: This is a particular type of chemical modifier for electrothermal AAS.

basicPropertyValues.val: Substance added together with the sample or standards in electrothermal atomic absorption spectroscopy that is refractory, or forms a refractory species (e.g., a carbide), and thus does not need to be renewed for several atomization cycles.

comments: The discharge is blown through a suitable orifice to form a plasma jet. The high-temperature, electric field-free gaseous region is designed as the region of observation.

basicPropertyValues.val: Temperature governing the number density of atomic species in their ground state and excited states following a Boltzmann distribution.

Gas streams used to maintain and stabilize the inductively-coupled plasma. The external stream is the main constituent of the plasma and confines the plasma avoiding melting of the torch walls; the intermediate gas stream keeps the plasma at a given height above the top of the torch and, the central stream carries the aerosol and promotes its injection in the plasma central channel.

Inductively-coupled plasma volume where there is a maximum interaction between the electromagnetic field and the plasma gas (mostly argon). This is the plasma’s hottest area and has a toroidal configuration.
Temperature associated with the energy level of plasma ions.
Condition for which the temperatures estimated from different particles (atoms, molecules, ions, electrons) constituting a plasma are locally coincident.

comments: The main process leading to plasma shielding is the absorption of the laser energy by electrons (inverse Bremsstrahlung) and multiphoton ionization (mainly relevant for shorter laser wavelengths).

basicPropertyValues.val: Prevention of laser pulse energy from reaching a sample surface as a result of the presence of a laser-induced plasma.

comments: The time elapsed between initiation and extinction of the plasma ranges from tenths of microseconds to a few milliseconds.

basicPropertyValues.val: Extinction of the plasma after a laser pulse as a consequence of self-absorption (quenching) and recombination of electrons and ions.

Sample support made of graphite that is inserted into the atomizer tube in electrothermal atomic absorption spectroscopy. The sample, a liquid or a solid, is deposited onto this platform, from which it undergoes all the transformations leading to atomization. The use of a platform delays atomization, until a more stabilized temperature in the gas phase is reached.

comments: Most common designs include cross flow, concentric, parallel path, entrained and Babington and V Groove.

basicPropertyValues.val: Nebulizers for which the aerosol generation principle is based on the exposure of the liquid sample to a high velocity gas stream.
Inductively-coupled plasma volume where tertiary aerosols suffer from complete solvent evaporation, element salt vaporization and dissociation into atoms.

comments: Usually, primary aerosols contain coarse droplets, they are polydisperse in terms of drop diameters and they are turbulent.
Pulse energies range from microjoules to millijoules for Q-switched lasers, whereas mode-locked lasers achieve much lower pulse energies (picojoules, nanojoules or sometimes several microjoules).

basicPropertyValues.val: Total optical energy content of a laser pulse. Integral of optical power over pulse duration.

comments: A pulsed laser produces no continuous optical wave.

basicPropertyValues.val: Laser system that emits electromagnetic radiation in the form of pulses of a defined and constant duration.
Graph of absorbance against pyrolysis temperature in electrothermal atomic absorption spectroscopy.

comments: These can be heated externally or positioned in a flame (see flame in flame atomic spectroscopy).

basicPropertyValues.val: Atomizer that is used to atomize those elements that form volatile species (e.g., hydrides) at relatively low temperatures (e.g., \(\pu{1000^{\circ}C}\) or below).

comments: This configuration yields lower sensitivities than the axial viewing mode.

basicPropertyValues.val: Inductively-coupled plasma optical emission spectrometer configuration in which the plasma and the entrance slit are perpendicular and from which the signal is taken perpendicularly to the main plasma axis.
Component of an inductively-coupled plasma spectrometer responsible for the generation of alternating current in the radiofrequency portion of the electromagnetic spectrum (see table).

nodes.lbl: radiofrequency glow discharge optical emission spectroscopy

comments: The use of these frequencies establishes a negative direct current (DC)-bias voltage on the sample surface. The DC-bias is the result of an alternating current waveform that is centered about negative potential; as such it more or less represents the average potential residing on the sample surface. Radio-frequency has ability to appear to flow through insulators (non-conductive materials).

basicPropertyValues.val: Optical emission spectroscopy in which a radiofrequency-powered glow discharge is operated with frequencies in the low megahertz range.
Intensity transmitted by the reference medium in a double-beam spectrometer.
Incident power that is not absorbed by the plasma.

comments: For laser systems with pulse duration in the nanosecond regime repetition rates range from \(\pu{1 Hz}\) to \(\pu{20 Hz}\), whereas for femtosecond laser systems increased repetition rates up to \(\pu{1000 Hz}\) are possible.
SI unit: \(\pu{Hz}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: Number of laser pulses emitted by a pulsed laser system per unit time.

comments: The incident photon energy is selected for resonance with an X-ray absorption edge of the system, such that the observed shifts in momentum and energy provide element-specific chemical sensitivity, with the capacity to distinguish the same element located at inequivalent sites.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement method of inelastic X-ray spectroscopy that uses a hard or soft X-ray beam to excite transitions of core-level electrons into empty energy levels. The subsequent transition of an electron into the core state is accompanied by X-ray emission with characteristic momentum and energy.

comments: For a gas composed of a single atomic species, the Saha equation is written: \[(n_{i+1}/n_{i}) n_{\rm{e}} = 2\lambda^{-3}(g_{i+1}/g_{i}) \exp[-(\epsilon_{i + 1} - \epsilon_{i})/kT]\] where \(n_{i}\) is the number density of atoms with \(i\) electrons removed, \(g_{i}\) is the degeneracy of the \(i^{\rm{th}}\) state, \(\epsilon_{i}\) is the ionization energy of the \(i^{\rm{th}}\) state, \(n_{\rm{e}}\) is the number density of electrons, \(\lambda\) is the thermal de Broglie wavelength of an electron, \(k\) is the Boltzmann constant, and \(T\) is the thermodynamic temperature of the gas.

The thermal de Broglie wavelength is given by: \[\lambda = \sqrt{\frac{h^{2}}{2\uppi m_{\rm{e}} kT}}\] where \(h\) is the Planck constant, \(k\) the Boltzmann constant, \(T\) temperature, and \(m_{\rm{e}}\) the mass of an electron.

basicPropertyValues.val: Equation that relates the ionization state of an element present in a gas in thermal equilibrium to the temperature and the pressure of the medium.
Intensity transmitted by the atomizer when the latter is supplied with the sample solution or a reference solution.
Buffer containing interfering element(s) in sufficient quantity to reach the limit of enhancement or dispersion (i.e., saturation) of the interference curve.

Sequential spectrometers use a dispersive element (grating) in combination with entrance and exit slits for selection of specific wavelengths. Geometric arrangements include the Czerny-Turner and the Ebert-geometry, both offering high resolution measurements. However, they do not permit simultaneous recording of different spectral lines, even for single emission line intensity, and adjacent spectral background has also to be measured sequentially.
Intensity transmitted by the atomizer when the latter is supplied with the solvent blank.
Solvent condensation on solid particles or droplets contained in an aerosol.
Mass of solvent, both in liquid and vapour forms, reaching an inductively-coupled plasma per unit of time.

comments: In the case of flame atomic spectroscopy, the term "flame background" is used.

basicPropertyValues.val: Electromagnetic radiation, within the bandpass used, emitted by, and/or in the case of atomic absorption spectroscopy, absorbed in, the atomizer when nothing is supplied to the atomizer but the gases involved in its operation.

comments: A distinction is made between lines corresponding to transition of neutral atoms (e.g., \(\ce{Ba I}\ \pu{553.548 nm}\) and \(\pu{577.762 nm}\)) and ions (e.g., \(\ce{Ba II}\ \pu{455.403 nm}\)).
The radiation is centred on a peak whose wavelength characterizes the line and which corresponds to the emission or absorption maximum.

basicPropertyValues.val: In atomic spectroscopy, a very narrow band of frequencies of electromagnetic radiation emitted or absorbed by atoms, which undergo a single electronic transition.
Chamber of a nebulizer in which the sprayed liquid is converted to mist. Some of the droplets of this mist may evaporate, coalesce, or deposit in the chamber and subsequently drain away as waste.

comments: Si unit \(\pu{kg s-1}\). Common unit \(\pu{\upmu g s-1}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: Mass of material removed from a sample surface in unit time.

Stoppage to the otherwise constant flow of argon gas to the atomizer in electrothermal atomic absorption spectroscopy, that can be programmed to occur during atomization, for the purpose of increasing the residence time of the analyte atoms and thus the associated signal.
X-ray spectroscopy performed using a high intensity, continuous polychromatic synchrotron X-ray source.

comments: Such aerosols are finer, less polydispersed and less turbulent than primary aerosols.

basicPropertyValues.val: Aerosol that reaches an inductively-coupled plasma.
Procedures whereby an aerosol is produced at a high temperature, for example by sparks, arcs, furnaces, lasers, cathodic sputtering or electron-beam.

comments: Although this technique offers highest detection power for most volatile elements its use in routine applications is still limited by the analytical challenges posed by the transient nature of the analyte signal.
The process causes evaporation of the sample constituents in accordance to their boiling-points.

basicPropertyValues.val: Process in glow-discharge atomic emission spectroscopy in which sample volatilization occurs by heating due to sample bombardment with argon ions.

Measurement method of laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy in which the emitted radiation is monitored with time resolution sufficiently high to resolve different stages in the lifetime of the laser-induced plasma.
Liquid-sample introduction system able to achieve \(\pu{100\%}\) transport efficiency.
Mass of analyte entering the atomizer of a flame atomic spectrometer or the plasma of an inductively-coupled plasma spectrometer divided by the mass of analyte entering the dispersion device.
Nebulizers whose aerosol generation principle is based on the transfer of the energy from a vibrating transducer to the liquid sample.

Electrothermal atomic absorption spectroscopy in which the sample is deposited directly onto the wall of the electrothermal atomizer tube, from which it undergoes all the transformations leading to atomization.

Time required for the output signal of an inductively-coupled plasma spectrometer for a given analyte to fall back to baseline levels from the end of sampling time and/or after introducing a blank solution.
Spectrum comprising the continuum Bremsstrahlung and the most energetic characteristic spectral lines defined by differences in binding energy between electron energy levels.

comments: AMTIRs are hard but can be brittle.

basicPropertyValues.val: Amorphous glasses made from elements of groups 4, 5 and 6 of the Periodic Table that transmit infrared radiation.

Modulation of the amplitude of a beam of electromagnetic radiation; by the movement of a moving mirror in a rapid scan Fourier-transform spectrometer or by a mechanical chopper in other spectrometers.
Raman scattering by the anisotropic part of the derived polarizability tensor.

Changes in real refractive index of a material in the vicinity of an absorption band in which real refractive index decreases markedly with decreasing wavenumber on the high wavenumber side of an absorption band, then increases rapidly through the band centre and decreases markedly on the low wavenumber side of the band, before resuming normal dispersion at wavenumbers far from the band.
Raman band with a depolarization ratio greater than \(\pu{0.75}\), as is frequently observed in surface-enhanced resonance Raman spectroscopy.
Raman scattering of electromagnetic radiation in which the scattered radiation has greater energy (greater wavenumber) than the exciting radiation.
Rotor whose three principal moments of inertia are all different.

comments: APTs have been widely used in the analysis of infrared absorption intensities.
SI unit: \(\pu{C}\). Common unit: \(\pu{D Å-1 \approx 3.33564E-30 C}\).
The rows correspond to different components of the dipole moment and the columns to \(x\), \(y\ (\rm{g})\) and \(z\) displacements.

basicPropertyValues.val: 3 × 3 tensor that gives the change in the components of the molecular dipole moment when the atom is displaced in three-dimensional space.

comments: Attenuated total reflection occurs where the material absorbs. The resulting spectrum resembles an absorption spectrum of the sample.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement method of vibrational spectroscopy based on internal reflection from an absorbing material at angles of incidence at or above the critical angle (attenuated total reflection).

comments: For a given band, the band shape is independent of the band height in Raman spectra, infrared absorption spectra and pATR spectra. The band shape changes if the band height changes in infrared transmission spectra or attenuated total reflection spectra.

basicPropertyValues.val: Description of the profile of a spectral band.

comments: Historically, a Bragg filter was a colloidal dispersion of spheres in a regular close packed array, which selectively diffracts/reflects wavelengths that satisfy the Bragg diffraction criterion for the lattice but transmits all other wavelengths. Now largely superseded by Volume Bragg Gratings, where photo-induced modulation of the refractive index of the filter medium is used to form a volume phase hologram with reflecting planes separated by a well-defined spacing. In each case, angle tuning is used to match the laser wavelength to the Bragg diffraction condition. The filter can be manufactured either as a notch filter, which transmits wavelengths either side of the laser line, or as an edge filter, which only transmits wavelengths longer than the laser line (i.e., Raman light subject to Stokes scattering).

basicPropertyValues.val: Optical filter used, for example, to attenuate Rayleigh scattering while transmitting light subject to Raman shift.
Spectral region of an interferogram around zero-path-difference where intensity is greatest.

comments: The Christiansen effect frequently causes strong absorption bands from coarsely ground particles to be distorted due to the change in refractive index associated with the anomalous dispersion of the refractive index through the absorption region.

basicPropertyValues.val: Collections of solid particles that are transparent to electromagnetic radiation of a particular wavelength and are slightly larger than the wavelength of the radiation transmit poorly due to reflection and scattering from the interfaces. The transmission increases markedly at wavenumbers at which the refractive index of the particles is close to that of the surrounding medium.

comments: Such filters have been made from quartz particles in air, immersed in \(\ce{CCl4}\), or immersed in mixtures of \(\ce{CCl4}\) and \(\ce{CS2}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: Optical filter based on the Christiansen effect.

comments: The Raman scattered radiation emerges as a laser beam instead of being scattered into three dimensions, thus greatly enhancing the sensitivity over that in normal Raman scattering.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement method of Raman spectroscopy that uses third-order susceptibility and is one of several four-wave mixing spectroscopies. The excitation is through lasers of wavenumber \(\tilde{ u}_{1}\) and \(\tilde{ u}_{2}\), which coincide spatially and temporally in the sample and produce an output laser of wavenumber \(\tilde{ u}_{3} = 2\tilde{ u}_{1} - \tilde{ u}_{2}\).

comments: Combination band results from a combination transition.
Combination transitions are either sum or difference transitions, although some authors restrict them to sum transitions.

basicPropertyValues.val: Transition in which more than one vibration changes its degree of excitation; i.e., in which more than one vibrational quantum number changes.

comments: Continuous scan interferometer is typically used for Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy.
In rapid-scan interferometers, the rate of change of optical path difference is above \(\pu{0.05 cm s-1}\), high enough that no additional modulation is needed.

In slow scan interferometers, the rate of change of optical path difference is less than \(\pu{0.05 cm s-1}\) and a mechanical chopper or some other ancillary modulation is frequently used to provide an adequate modulation frequency.

basicPropertyValues.val: Interferometer in which the optical path difference is continually changed.
Coupling between rotational and vibrational molecular motion caused by Coriolis forces.

comments: SI unit: \(\ce{N}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: In vibrational theory, the motion of a polyatomic molecule is usually initially regarded as the independent superposition of a rotation and a vibration, with the vibration considered in a coordinate system that rotates with the molecule. This initial treatment must be corrected for centrifugal forces and for Coriolis forces. The Coriolis force on an atom is given by \(F_{\rm{Coriolis}} = 2m v_{\rm{a}} \omega \sin \varphi\), where \(m\) is the mass of the atom, \(v_{\rm{a}}\) is its apparent velocity in the rotating coordinate system, \(\omega\) is the angular velocity of the coordinate system, and \(\varphi\) is the angle between the velocity vector and the axis of rotation.

comments: If \(n_{2}\) and \(n_{1}\) are the refractive indices, and \(n_{2} > n_{1}\), at the boundary, \(\sin \theta_{\rm{c}} = n_1/n_2\).

basicPropertyValues.val: Smallest angle of incidence at which total internal reflection occurs.
Vibration in which the dominant change from equilibrium is in one or more valence angles.

comments: In normal Raman scattering with linearly polarized exciting radiation, \(\rho \le 0.75\) for totally symmetric vibrations and \(\rho = 0.75\) for all other vibrations.

basicPropertyValues.val: Raman intensity with the electric vector of the scattered electromagnetic radiation perpendicular to that of the incident radiation divided by the Raman intensity with electric vectors parallel.
Raman band with depolarization ratio \(\rho = 0.75\) for linear polarized incident radiation in normal Raman spectroscopy.

comments: A difference band or difference tone results from a difference transition.

basicPropertyValues.val: Combination transition that does not start at the ground state and in which at least one vibration decreases and at least one vibration increases its degree of excitation; i.e., a transition in which more than one vibrational quantum number changes and at least one becomes smaller.

Measuring instrument for Raman spectroscopy incorporating a dish-shaped cell that is divided by a vertical partition through its middle to allow different liquids in its two halves. It is rotated about a vertical axis through its centre and the Raman scattered radiation from each half is measured alternately. With a standard liquid in one half and a sample in the other it is used to determine Raman scattering intensities relative to the standard.

comments: The reference spectrum may be chosen in many ways; e.g., it may be the average over \(\tau\), of the observed spectrum, or it may be zero.

basicPropertyValues.val: Spectrum of a material under the influence of an applied external perturbation represented by a variable \(\tau\), relative to a reference spectrum.

comments: Electrical anharmonicity should not be confused with mechanical anharmonicity.

basicPropertyValues.val: Influence of terms that are of \(2^{\rm{nd}}\) and higher order in the normal coordinate \(Q\) in the expansion of the electric dipole moment.

comments: Electrical harmonicity should not be confused with mechanical harmonicity.

basicPropertyValues.val: Influence of the linear term, \(\Sigma_{k} (\partial \boldsymbol{\mu}/\partial Q_{k}) Q_{k}\), in the expansion of the electric dipole moment. \(Q\) is the normal coordinate.

comments: EELS is used for the study of electronic states and has an energy resolution of \(\pu{0.25 eV}\) or better (corresponding to an approximate wavenumber of \(\pu{2000 cm-1}\)).

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement method of vibrational spectroscopy in which a constant-energy beam of electrons passes through or is reflected from a sample and the energy distribution in the transmitted or reflected beam is analysed to give a spectrum of number of electrons against electron energy loss.

comments: In Note 1, \(R\), are vibrational coordinates such as bond stretching, angle deformation, or torsion about a bond.

The original EOPs were \(\mu_{k}^{\circ}\), the equilibrium bond moment, and \(\partial \mu_{k}/\partial R_{t}\), the change in the electric dipole moment of bond \(k\) with change in internal displacement coordinate \(t\). A later and completely equivalent formulation uses equilibrium atomic charges, \(q_{\alpha}^{\rm{o}}\), and charge fluxes, \(\partial q_{\alpha}/\partial R_{t}\), which are also called EOPs as well as ECCF for equilibrium charge, charge flux.

basicPropertyValues.val: Characteristic quantity used in the analysis of absolute infrared intensity data chosen on the assumption that the electric dipole moment of the molecule can be described as the vector sum of bond dipole moments.

comments: SI unit: rad = 1.

basicPropertyValues.val: Degree to which linearly polarized incident electromagnetic radiation becomes elliptically polarized in an absorbing optically active medium. \[\tan\;\psi = (E_{\rm{R}} - E_{\rm{L}})/(E_{\rm{R}} + E_{\rm{L}}) = \tanh (k^{\rm{L}} - k^{\rm{R}})\pi l/\lambda\] where \(E_{\rm{R}}\) and \(E_{\rm{L}}\) are the electric vectors of right and left circularly polarized radiation, \(k^{\rm{L}}\) and \(k^{\rm{R}}\) are the absorption indices of the sample for left and right circularly polarized radiation, \(\lambda\) is the wavelength of the radiation and \(l\) is the path-length through the medium.
Part of a standing-wave normal to a reflecting surface that extends beyond the reflecting surface when an electromagnetic wave undergoes total internal reflection.
Unexpected minimum or hole in a broad absorption band due to a gap being created in a broad distribution of states by Fermi resonance.
Graph of Raman intensity at the desired Raman shift against wavenumber of the excitation.
Measurement method of spectroscopy in which radiation is reflected from a sample of higher refractive index than that of the incident medium.

comments: In uniaxial crystals the optic axis coincides with the symmetry axis. The refractive index of the crystal is the same in all directions perpendicular to the optic axis but is different along the optic axis. Consequently, electromagnetic rays or waves that do not travel along the optic axis experience different refractive indices in different directions perpendicular to their direction of propagation. Two waves result, one has its electric vector perpendicular to the optic axis and forms the ordinary wave. The other is the extraordinary wave.

basicPropertyValues.val: In a uniaxial crystal electromagnetic radiation with electric vector oblique to the optic axis and which does not obey the normal laws of refraction.

comments: Fermi resonance is usually identified by the presence of more than one band of comparable intensity when only one fundamental is expected. Also seen as an Evans hole.
Traditionally, Fermi resonance was defined as the anharmonic interaction between a fundamental state and one or more overtone or combination transitions.

basicPropertyValues.val: Cubic anharmonic resonance (see anharmonicity), i.e., any interaction caused by cubic terms in the vibrational potential energy.
Free spectral range divided by resolution.
Infrared and Raman bands that are characteristic of a particular molecule rather than a functional group.

comments: The fingerprint region is often associated with the region of the mid-infrared or Raman spectrum of wavenumbers between \(\pu{1500 cm-1}\) and \(\pu{400 cm-1}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: Region of a spectrum that contains fingerprint bands as well as bands with characteristic group frequencies.
Infrared spectroscopy in which a Fourier-transform spectrometer is used to separate the transmitted electromagnetic radiation into its component wavenumbers.

comments: This technique usually uses near-infrared excitation.

basicPropertyValues.val: Raman spectroscopy in which a Fourier-transform spectrometer is used to separate the scattered electromagnetic radiation into its component wavenumbers.

comments: SI unit: \(\pu{m-1}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: For a Fabry-Perot or laser cavity, wavenumber interval between successive longitudinal cavity modes of vibration; \(\Delta \tilde{ u} = 1/(2nl)\), where \(l\) is the cavity spacing and \(n\) is the refractive index of the material in the cavity.

comments: Ideally the angle of incidence should be greater than \(\pu{80\!^{\circ}}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: Angle of incidence of a beam of electromagnetic radiation greater than \(\pu{70\!^{\circ}}\).

comments: The frequency is usually given as a wavenumber.

basicPropertyValues.val: Frequency in vibrational spectroscopy that is characteristic of a particular chemical functional group.

comments: SI unit: \(\pu{m-1}\). Common unit: \(\pu{cm-1}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: Coefficient of (\( u + ½\)) in the vibrational term value, determined by the harmonic terms in the vibrational potential energy.

comments: Such mechanisms do not require an ensemble of spectroscopically non-equivalent molecules of the same species. Such mechanisms are the natural line width, which is usually negligible in vibrational spectroscopy, and intra- or inter- molecular interactions, including anharmonic vibrational interactions (see anharmonicity), that reduce the lifetime of the excited state.

basicPropertyValues.val: Line-broadening by mechanisms that affect every molecule of the same species in the sample in the same way.

comments: A hot band arises from a hot transition.
A hot transition has the same changes in vibrational quantum numbers as a fundamental, overtone transition, or sum transition but it originates in an excited vibrational state not the ground state.

basicPropertyValues.val: Electronic transition between an excited state and a state in which all vibrational quantum numbers are the same or greater.

Raman spectroscopy in which scattering occurs through hyperpolarizabilities. A two-photon technique in which an intense pulsed beam of electromagnetic radiation is focused onto the sample. When sufficient power is present in the pulse, two photons may interact with the one molecule to create a virtual state at double the frequency of the laser excitation. Raman scattering from this virtual state to an excited vibrational state of the ground state then occurs.
Measurement method to obtain information about the spatial composition of a sample by obtaining a spectrum at each spatially resolved point of the sample.

comments: In crystallography, a rotation-inversion axis, which is a symmetry element such that rotation by \(2\pi/n\) about the axis followed by inversion through the centre of symmetry transforms an object into itself.

basicPropertyValues.val: In spectroscopy, a rotation-reflection axis, which is a symmetry element such that rotation by \(2\pi/n\) about the axis followed by reflection through a plane perpendicular to the axis transforms an object into itself.

comments: IETS yields vibrational spectra of adsorbates with high resolution (better than \(\pu{0.5 meV}\)) and low limit of detection (below \(\pu{E13}\) molecules are required to provide a spectrum).

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement method of vibrational spectroscopy to obtain spectra of molecules on metal oxide surfaces.

comments: If there is no ambiguity the term 'infrared' is used for the mid-infrared region.

The infrared range is sub-divided into three regions: near-infrared: \(\pu{780 nm}\) to \(\pu{2.5 \upmu m}\) (\(\pu{12800 cm-1}\) to \(\pu{400 cm-1}\)); mid-infrared: \(\pu{2.5 \upmu m}\) to \(\pu{25 \upmu m}\) (\(\pu{4000 cm-1}\) to \(\pu{400 cm-1}\)) and far infrared: \(\pu{25 \upmu m}\) to \(\pu{1000 \upmu m}\) (\(\pu{400 cm-1}\) to \(\pu{10 cm-1}\)).

The wavelength regions given are commonly used in chemistry and relate to working ranges of infrared spectrometers. Note that in other disciplines (e.g., astronomy) the terms are defined for different ranges.

basicPropertyValues.val: Electromagnetic radiation of wavelength between approximately \(\pu{780 nm}\) and \(\pu{1000 \upmu m}\) or of wavenumber between approximately \(\pu{13000 cm-1}\) and \(\pu{10 cm-1}\).

comments: Without qualification, 'infrared spectroscopy' usually refers to use of the mid-infrared (wavelength range \(\pu{2.5}\) to \(\pu{25 \upmu m}\), wavenumber range (\(\pu{4000 cm-1}\) to \(\pu{400 cm-1}\)) region of the electromagnetic spectrum (see table).

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement principle of vibrational spectroscopy using infrared radiation.

Line-broadening by mechanisms that arise from an ensemble of spectroscopically non-equivalent molecules of the same species. Such molecules exist, for example, when molecules occupy non-equivalent sites in a condensed phase, and when gaseous molecules have different velocities and, thus, shift the observed wavenumber differently through the Doppler effect.

comments: A spectrum of interference fringes is termed a channel spectrum.
Interference fringes are frequently observed in the transmission spectrum of a cell with flat windows and in non-scattering polymer films.

basicPropertyValues.val: Sinusoidal intensity variation due to interference of electromagnetic radiation that undergoes multiple reflection between two flat and parallel surfaces.

comments: The interference record contains a part that is constant and a part that varies with the path difference.

basicPropertyValues.val: Record of the signal from the detector of a two-beam interferometer as the optical path difference between the two beams is varied.
Pattern formed by wave interference produced by an interferometer, especially one represented on a screen or chart recorder.
Reflection of electromagnetic radiation from a material of lesser refractive index than that of the incident medium.

comments: The sample is mounted in optical contact with the element.

basicPropertyValues.val: Transparent or semi-transparent material of high refractive index that carries infrared radiation to a sample in internal reflection and attenuated total reflection measurements.

Raman scattering showing absorption when Stokes Raman scattering exceeds anti-Stokes Raman scattering, in an experiment in which a sample is simultaneously illuminated by coincident beams from a continuum source and a pulse laser at \(\tilde{ u}_{0}\). Energy is absorbed from the continuum at \(\tilde{ u}_{0} + \tilde{ u}_{\rm{s}}\) where \(\tilde{ u}_{\rm{s}}\) is the wavenumber of a Raman-active vibration in the sample that is excited by this process, and this energy is emitted at \(\tilde{ u}_{0}\).
Variant of spatially offset Raman spectroscopy in which a sample is illuminated with a ring of laser light and the Raman scattering is collected from the centre of the ring.

comments: IRTRAN 1 to IRTRAN 5 are hot-pressed forms of \(\ce{MgF2}\), \(\ce{CdF2}\), \(\ce{MgO}\), \(\ce{ZnSe}\) and \(\ce{ZnS}\), respectively.
IRTRAN is a registered trade mark of Eastman Kodak Co.

basicPropertyValues.val: Kinds of crystal transparent to infrared radiation used as windows and filters in infrared spectroscopy.

Aperture in the optics of a Fourier-transform spectrometer, typically between the source and the interferometer, designed to be the limiting aperture when no other optical element such as the detector serves this purpose.

comments: Two displacement coordinates must share a common atom if they are to undergo kinetic coupling.

basicPropertyValues.val: Coupling of vibrational displacements through terms in the vibrational kinetic energy.

comments: KRS-5 transmits well down to \(\pu{200 cm-1}\). It is practically insoluble in water but its refractive index is rather high (approximately 2.35). It is rather plastic and deforms with time, and it is poisonous.

basicPropertyValues.val: Eutectic (\(\pu{42 \% TlBr, 58 \% TlI}\)) mixture of thallium bromide and thallium iodide transparent to infrared radiation used as window in infrared spectroscopy.

comments: Theoretically \(f(R_{\infty})\) equals the ratio of the linear decadic absorption coefficient to the scattering coefficient. Under the assumptions of the Kubelka Munk theory, if the scattering coefficient at a given wavenumber is a constant for a given set of samples, \(f(R_{\infty})\) is directly proportional to the product of the absorption coefficient and concentration of each component of a mixture, analogous to the behaviour of absorbance under Beer’s law.

basicPropertyValues.val: \(f(R_{\infty}) = (1 – R_{\infty})^{2}/2R_{\infty}\), where \(R_{\infty}\) is the diffuse reflectance from a sample of infinite depth.

comments: The lifetime may be limited by the natural lifetime, by collisions, as in pressure broadening, or by anharmonic vibrational interactions as in phonon-phonon collisions in solids.

basicPropertyValues.val: Homogeneous line-broadening due to the limited lifetime of energy states involved in a transition.

comments: For highly excited \(\ce{CH}\) stretching vibrations anharmonic interactions mix the normal modes of vibration to the point that each observed mode of vibration behaves as a local mode.

basicPropertyValues.val: Mode of vibration localized in one type of bond.

comments: SI unit: \(\pu{J-1 C2 m2 mol-1}\).
The imaginary molar polarizability shows the absorption band free from long range dielectric effects that distort the band shapes of very strong absorptions.

basicPropertyValues.val: Defined under the assumption of the Lorentz local field by the Lorentz-Lorenz formula: \[\hat{\alpha}_{\rm{m}}(\tilde{ u}) = 3V_{\rm{m}}\epsilon_{0} \frac{\hat{\epsilon}(\tilde{ u}) - 1}{\hat{\epsilon}(\tilde{ u}) + 2} = 3V_{\rm{m}}{\epsilon}_{0}\,\frac{\hat{n}^{2}(\tilde{ u}) - 1}{\hat{n}^{2}(\tilde{ u}) + 2}\] where \(V_{\rm{m}}\) is the molar volume and \(\hat{\epsilon}\) and \(\boldsymbol{\hat{n}}\) are the complex dielectric constant and refractive index, respectively. To allow description of absorption, \(\hat{\alpha}_{\rm{m}}(\tilde{ u})\) is complex: \(\hat{\alpha}_{\rm{m}}(\tilde{ u}) = \alpha_{\rm{m}}'(\tilde{ u}) + \rm{i}\alpha_{\rm{m}}''(\tilde{ u})\).

comments: Mechanical anharmonicity should not be confused with electrical anharmonicity.

basicPropertyValues.val: Influence of cubic and higher-order terms in vibrational potential energy.

comments: Mechanical harmonicity should not be confused with electrical harmonicity.

basicPropertyValues.val: Influence of quadratic terms in vibrational potential energy.

comments: SI unit: \(\pu{rad m2 mol-1}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: Ellipticity divided by the amount concentration of the optically active absorbing material and by the path-length at temperature (\(t\)) and wavelength (\(\lambda\)).
Decrease in measurement uncertainty obtained by measuring intensity at many different wavelengths simultaneously, as is done, for example, in Fourier-transform spectroscopy.

comments: If the excited state \(n\) can only emit spontaneously to a single lower state \(m\) the natural linewidth is \(\pu{1.86E-38}\ \tilde{\nu}_{mn}^3 \langle m|\boldsymbol{\mu}|n \rangle^{2}\), when the transition wavenumber \(\tilde{\nu}_{mn}\) is in \(\pu{cm-1}\) and the dipole moment \(\mu\) is in Debye (\(\pu{1D \approx 3.335E-30 C m}\)). In the infrared, typical natural linewidths are approximately \(\pu{E-7 cm-1}\).
The natural linewidth, measured as the full width half maximum equals \(1/(2\pi c_{0} \Delta t)\), where \(\Delta t\) is the natural lifetime of the excited state.

basicPropertyValues.val: Line width of a molecular spectral band that arises from the probability of spontaneous emission in the absence of radiation fields and interaction with other molecules or entities.

comments: The region is often divided into the silicon region between \(\pu{12800 cm-1}\) and \(\pu{9000 cm-1}\) (\(\pu{800 nm}\) and \(\pu{1100 nm}\)) and the lead sulfide region between \(\pu{9000 cm-1}\) and \(\pu{4000 cm-1}\) (\(\pu{1100 nm}\) and \(\pu{2500 nm}\)), where the names reflect the common detector for the region.

basicPropertyValues.val: Infrared radiation of which vacuum wavenumbers range from approximately \(\pu{12800 cm-1}\) to \(\pu{4800 cm-1}\) and wavelengths range from approximately \(\pu{780 nm}\) to \(\pu{2500 nm}\).

comments: These methods are mainly used to obtain adequate optical throughput for process measurement and monitoring.

basicPropertyValues.val: Kinds of infrared spectroscopy in which the effect of the sample on the radiation from the source is measured as a whole without exploring the dependence on wavenumber.

Formal mathematical description of a normal vibration. When the potential energy, \(V\), is harmonic and the kinetic energy, \(T\), is calculated in the limit of infinitesimally small displacements, the normal coordinates are defined as independent entities such that '(for non-linear molecules)'\[V = ½\sum_{k=1}^{3N-6}\lambda_{k}Q_{k}^{2}\ {\rm{and}}\ T = ½\sum_{k=1}^{3N-6}\dot Q_{k}^{2}\]where \(\lambda_{k}\) is the \(k^{\rm{th}}\) eigenvalue and \(\dot {Q}\) is \(\partial Q/\partial t\). Normal coordinate \(Q_{k}\) is related to the internal displacement coordinates, \(R_{i}\), through the elements, \(L_{ik} = \partial R_{i}/\partial Q_{k}\) of the \(k^{\rm{th}}\) column of the eigenvector matrix \(\boldsymbol{L}\). Normal coordinates are not independent when the potential energy is anharmonic, or the displacements are not infinitesimal.
Calculation of the normal modes of vibrations of a molecule or crystal under the assumptions that the potential energy is harmonic and the displacements from equilibrium are infinitesimal.

nodes.lbl: normal dispersion of the refractive index

basicPropertyValues.val: Slow decrease of real refractive index of a material in a non-absorbing spectral region far from regions of strong absorption as the wavenumber decreases.
Incidence of a beam of electromagnetic radiation when the angle of incidence \(\theta = \pu{0\!^{\circ}}\), i.e., the incident radiation beam is normal to the surface.

comments: Normal modes of vibration is an idealized concept that has proved extremely useful in analysing spectra in vibrational spectroscopy.

basicPropertyValues.val: One of the \(3N - 6\) (\(3N - 5\) for a linear molecule) modes of vibration that would add to give the total vibrational motion in a molecule if the interatomic potential were strictly quadratic in the displacements from equilibrium.

comments: Normalized tunnelling intensity is plotted against the bias voltage to report inelastic electron tunnelling spectroscopy data.

basicPropertyValues.val: Second differential of intensity with respect to bias voltage divided by first differential of intensity with respect to bias voltage.

comments: SI unit: \(\pu{m}\). Common unit: \(\pu{\upmu m}\).
\(\mu_{\beta}\) is the reciprocal of the linear Napierian absorption coefficient.

basicPropertyValues.val: Depth in a sample at which the intensity of an incident beam is reduced to \(1/\rm{e}\) of its value at the surface of the sample.
Collective name for the real refractive index, \(n\) and the absorption index (imaginary refractive index), \(k\).

Spectrometer in which the ratio of the radiant power in the two beams at each wavenumber is measured opto-mechanically by inserting a linear optical attenuator into the reference beam until the two signals measured by the detector are equal, then measuring the displacement of the optical attenuator.

comments: SI unit: \(\pu{m}\). Common unit: \(\pu{cm}\).
The term optical retardation is derived from 'phase retardation', which refers to the change in the phase of the electromagnetic radiation in the interferometer.

basicPropertyValues.val: Path-length difference between the arms of a two-beam interferometer.
Wavelength dependence of the angle of rotation of the plane of linearly-polarized radiation when transmitted through optically active materials.

comments: In uniaxial crystals the optic axis coincides with the symmetry axis. The refractive index of the crystal is the same in all directions perpendicular to the optic axis but is different along the optic axis. Consequently, electromagnetic rays or waves that do not travel along the optic axis experience different refractive indices in different directions perpendicular to their direction of propagation. Two waves result, one has its electric vector perpendicular to the optic axis and forms the ordinary wave. The other is the extraordinary wave.

basicPropertyValues.val: In a uniaxial crystal electromagnetic radiation with electric vector perpendicular to the optic axis and which obeys the normal laws of refraction.

comments: An overtone band results from an overtone transition.

basicPropertyValues.val: Transition between the ground state and a state in which a single mode of vibration is multiply excited.

comments: The term is used to avoid the confusing, but common and incorrect, practice of calling it the absorbance spectrum.

basicPropertyValues.val: \(-\log_{10}\) of the spectrum obtained in attenuated total reflection spectroscopy.

comments: Photoacoustic saturation arises when the sample is optically opaque and thermally thin, i.e., when the thermal diffusion depth, \(L\), is greater than the optical absorption depth, \(\mu_{\beta}\), and less than the sample thickness. The condition may be relieved by increasing the modulation frequency sufficiently that \(L\) becomes less than \(\mu_{\beta}\), i.e., that the sample becomes thermally thick.

basicPropertyValues.val: Condition in photoacoustic spectroscopy in which all bands with greater than a certain absorption intensity appear to have the same intensity.
Measurement method of spectroscopy in which the absorption of electromagnetic radiation by a sample is detected as a result of the heat generated by the absorption.
Raman band with depolarization ratio \(\rho \le 0.75\) for linear polarized incident radiation in normal Raman spectroscopy.

Coupling of vibrational displacements through terms in the vibrational potential energy. The second-order (quadratic) terms cause harmonic potential coupling while the cubic and higher terms cause anharmonic potential coupling.

Polarization when electromagnetic radiation is incident upon a surface with its electric vector in the plane of incidence and, therefore, inclined to the reflecting surface unless the incidence is normal.

comments: At pressures sufficiently low that the line width is far smaller than the line wavelength, the line width increases linearly with pressure, the broadening is homogeneous and the line shape is Lorentzian.

basicPropertyValues.val: Increase in the line width of a spectral line of a gas due to molecular collisions and other intermolecular interactions that reduce the lifetime of an excited state.

comments: A QCL can be used as a source for infrared spectroscopy.

In practice, the circular polarization of the exciting beam, or of the scattered beam, or of both beams simultaneously, may be selected. Raman optical activity is usually specified as 'right minus left' circular polarizations, in unfortunate contrast to the 'left minus right' specification that is universal in vibrational circular polarization and other forms of optical activity.

basicPropertyValues.val: Phenomenon that vibrations in chiral molecules and materials Raman scattering right circularly polarized incident radiation to a different extent than left circularly polarized incident radiation.

comments: Normal Raman scattering occurs through changes in polarizability of a molecule during a vibration, not the hyper-polarizabilities, and is excited by radiation that is not in resonance with electronic transitions in the sample.
The energy of the scattered photon can be lesser (Stokes Raman scattering) or greater (anti-Stokes Raman scattering) than that of the incident photon.

basicPropertyValues.val: Inelastic scattering of electromagnetic radiation by molecules that are excited to higher energy levels.

comments: SI unit: \(\pu{m-1}\). Common unit: \(\pu{cm-1}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: Difference in wavenumber between the incident and scattered electromagnetic radiation in Raman spectroscopy.

comments: Raman scattered light occurs at wavelengths that are shifted from the incident light by the energies of molecular vibrations.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement principle of vibrational spectroscopy based on Raman scattering.

comments: Commonly a Raman spectrum is obtained between approximately \(\pu{100 cm-1}\) and \(\pu{3500 cm-1}\) and is a complement to its counterpart mid-infrared spectrum.

basicPropertyValues.val: Graph of the intensity of scattered electromagnetic radiation in Raman spectroscopy against Raman shift.

comments: SI unit: \(\pu{m-1}\). Common unit: \(\pu{cm-1}\).
\(\Delta \tilde{\nu}\) is positive for Stokes Raman scattering and negative for anti-Stokes Raman scattering.

basicPropertyValues.val: Wavenumber of exciting electromagnetic radiation minus wavenumber of the scattered radiation.
Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy in which the optical path difference is continually changed at a rate of \(\pu{0.05 cm s-1}\) or greater.

comments: As the incident radiation beam travels nearly parallel to the sample surface, the electric vector of the radiation is then either parallel or nearly perpendicular to the surface.

basicPropertyValues.val: Reflection-absorption with very thin layers of an absorbing material on a metallic substrate and the angle of incidence between \(\pu{70\!^{\circ}}\) and \(\pu{90\!^{\circ}}\).

Raman scattering that occurs through the polarizability of a molecule, (not the hyperpolarizabilities) and is excited by electromagnetic radiation that is in resonance with electronic transitions or vibronic transitions in the sample.

comments: The most commonly observed branches for simple molecules are the \(\rm{P}\), \(\rm{Q}\) and \(\rm{R}\) branches in infrared spectroscopy and the \(\rm{O}\), \(\rm{Q}\) and \(\rm{S}\) branches in Raman spectroscopy.
\(\Delta J = J_{\rm{upper}} - J_{\rm{lower}} = -2, -1, 0, +1\ \rm{and}\ +2\) for the \(\rm{O}\), \(\rm{P}\), \(\rm{Q}\), \(\rm{R}\) and \(\rm{S}\) branches, respectively.

basicPropertyValues.val: Spectral lines in the rotation-vibration spectrum of a gas that derive from the same change in rotation quantum number, \(J\).
Spectrum that shows absorption or emission of radiation during transitions between rotational-vibrational states of a molecule.

comments: A common notation, due to Porto, is \(k_{\rm{i}}(p_{\rm{i}}\,p_{\rm{s}})k_{\rm{s}}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: Relation between the propagation directions, \(k_{\rm{i}}\), \(k_{\rm{s}}\), and the polarization directions, \(p_{\rm{i}}\), \(p_{\rm{s}}\), of the incident and scattered radiation, usually expressed in terms of laboratory-fixed or crystal-fixed Cartesian axes.

comments: Site splitting arises from the static intermolecular forces in the crystal.

basicPropertyValues.val: Appearance of more than one band in the spectrum of a crystal when only one is seen in that of the gas, when this splitting is attributed to either the molecule lying on a crystal site of lower symmetry than that of the gaseous molecule or to molecules occupying more than one type of crystal site. See crystal field splitting.

comments: SORS allows chemical analysis of objects beneath diffusely scattering surfaces, such as tissue, powders and translucent plastics.

basicPropertyValues.val: Measurement method of Raman spectroscopy in which the sample is illuminated at one location, and the Raman signal is collected from a different location on the sample surface.
Molecule whose three principal moments of inertia are all the same. An isotropic molecule.

Interferometer (typically used for Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy) in which the optical path difference is changed by a certain amount, held constant, or modulated if phase modulation is desired, while the signal at the current path difference is recorded, then the process is repeated.

Two-photon Raman scattering occurs when a picosecond pump beam is used to create a virtual state and a probe beam of a frequency to match the frequency of Stokes Raman scattering from the virtual state to a specific vibrational level. The Stokes emission is stimulated thus depopulating the virtual state very quickly and increasing the scattering efficiency for the chosen vibration by orders of magnitude. SRS is a non-linear process, so sufficient photons from both the pump and probe beams must be present on the molecule at the one time.
Raman scattering of electromagnetic radiation in which the scattered radiation has lesser energy (lesser wavenumber) than the exciting radiation.
Band resulting from a sum transition.
Combination transition between the ground state and a state in which more than one vibration is excited; i.e., a transition from the ground state in which more than one quantum number increases.
