Any of several autoimmune diseases that are caused by tumor-induced perturbations of the immune system with damaging effects on various organ systems (e.g. cancer-associated retinopathy, paraneoplastic neurological syndromes, paraneoplastic cutaneous syndromes). In most cases, autoantibodies generated by antitumor immunity are responsible for the tissue injury.
Site in the variable region of an antibody or T-cell receptor (TCR) that binds to an epitope of an antigen.

Immunoassay in which antibody is bound to the surface of microspheres. After incubation with the antigen-containing biological fluid, and subsequent manipulation, detection is usually performed by flow cytometry.

Assay for allergenicity in which an antibody is injected intradermally into a test animal followed at a later time (anywhere from \(\pu{3}\) to \(\pu{48 h}\)) with an intravenous injection of a mixture of a test antigen and a dye (typically Evans blue). Increased vascular permeability at the site of antigen-antibody reaction is visualized by extravasation of the dye.
Method of measuring antibody titer, in which antigen-coated erythrocytes are agglutinated by adding antibody specific for the antigen.
Immunization of an individual by the transfer of antibody synthesized in another individual.
Test for allergy that is performed by placing the suspected allergen in direct contact with the skin or mucosa.

Describing repetitive motifs of molecules such as lipopolysaccharide (LPS), peptidoglycan, lipoteichoic acids, and mannans, which are widely expressed by microbial pathogens but are not present on host tissues. They are therefore utilized by the pattern recognition receptors (PRRs) of the immune system to distinguish pathogens from self-antigens.

comments: Many of the NOD-like receptors (NLRs) are thought to serve as PRRs.

basicPropertyValues.val: Receptor found on many different cell types in the immune system that enables them to recognize pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs). Amongst the large number of different PRRs are the mannose receptor (CD206), macrophage scavenger receptor (CD204), and the toll-like receptors (TLRs).
Referring to vasculitis characterized by relatively little deposition of immunoglobulin (Ig) and complement factors, usually describing a form of glomerulonephritis.

comments: Other mucous membranes, as well as the skin, are usually affected and the disease may be fatal.

basicPropertyValues.val: Rare, serious autoimmune disease marked by successive outbreaks of blisters, which appear suddenly and disappear, leaving pigmented spots.

Structure consisting of four identical major histocompatibility complex (MHC)-encoded peptides, presenting four binding sites for biotin attached to the tail of the MHC molecule, and held together by fluorescent streptavidin.
Preparation of an immunologically active peptide found in a disease-causing organism or substance, or any of their products, which is specially treated for use in vaccination.
Structural feature found in major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I and class II heterodimeric proteins that can bind endogenous peptides.
Molecule produced by cytotoxic T cells and natural killer (NK) cells that, like complement component C9, polymerizes to form a pore in the membrane of the target cell leading to cell death.
Lymphoid tissue that forms the white pulp of the spleen.

Inflammatory reaction of the tissues surrounding a tooth (periodontium), usually resulting from the extension of gingival inflammation (gingivitis) into the periodontium, and involving inflammation and infection of the ligaments and bones that support the teeth.
Leukocyte derived from the peripheral circulatory system.

comments: PBMCs constitute between \(\pu{3}\) to \(\pu{8\%}\) of the leukocytes in the blood. In the tissues monocytes mature into different types of macrophages at different anatomical locations [see macrophage, resident(ial)].

basicPropertyValues.val: Monocyte produced by the bone marrow from hematopoietic stem cell precursors, circulating in the bloodstream for about one to three days before moving into tissues throughout the body.
Any of the lymphoid organs (see lymphoid tissue) other than the thymus.

Acute or chronic inflammatory neuropathy leading to demyelination and axonal damage of nerves and nerve roots associated with high-titeredautoantibodies against gangliosides [e.g., Guillain–Barré syndrome (GBS), Miller–Fisher syndrome, acute sensory ataxic neuropathy].
Specific immunological tolerance occurring outside of the primary lymphoid organs (see lymphoid tissue).

comments: This disease is associated with a variety of autoimmune endocrine diseases (e.g., Hashimoto thyroiditis, Addison disease, and autoimmune myasthenic syndromes).
This is the end stage of \(\pu{10}\) to \(\pu{15\%}\) of autoimmune gastritis.

basicPropertyValues.val: Disease in which the erythrocytes are abnormally formed, due to an inability to absorb vitamin \({\rm{B}}_{12}\). True pernicious anemia refers specifically to a disorder of atrophied parietal cells leading to absent intrinsic factor, resulting in an inability to absorb \({\rm{B}}_{12}\).
Autophagy selective for degradation of peroxisomes, which can be separated into macropexophagy and micropexophagy.
Part of the gut-associated lymphoid tissue (GALT) and found as a distinct lymphoid nodule, mainly in the small intestine.
Cell, especially of monocyte/macrophage or neutrophil lineage, that is specialized for the engulfment of cellular and particulate matter.

Method of quantifying phagocytosis in which yeast cells, stained with May–Grünwald stain, are incubated with macrophages, and subsequently, after a fixed time, yeast cells engulfed in the macrophages are counted.
Process by which particulate material is endocytosed by a cell.
Intracellular vacuole where killing and digestion of phagocytosed material occurs following the fusion of a phagosome with a lysosome.
Intracellular vacuole produced following invagination of the cell membrane around phagocytosed material.
Chromosome resulting from a reciprocal translocation between human chromosomes 9 and 22, most commonly associated with chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML).
Mitogenic phorbol ester that directly stimulates protein kinase C (PKC) and acts as a tumor promoter.

comments: One consequence of the signaling is B- and T-lymphocyte activation.

basicPropertyValues.val: Enzyme that cleaves phosphatidylinositol bisphosphate into diacylglycerol and inositol trisphosphate, leading to the activation of two major cell signaling pathways.
Type IV hypersensitivity reaction in which photoactivation of a substance produces a hapten that then acts as a sensitizer.

comments: Aftershave lotions, sunscreens, and certain topical sulfa drugs may be changed into allergens, while coal tar and certain oils used in manufacturing may become irritants after exposure to sunlight.

basicPropertyValues.val: Type of contact dermatitis arising when substances are transformed into either irritants or allergens upon exposure to light.

Skin reddening due to an abnormal reaction to sunlight, characteristic of systemic autoimmune diseases [e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD)], and cutaneous and subacute cutaneous lupus erythematosus.

comments: There is also an in vitro test using photoexposure of treated Balb c/3T3 cells followed by viability testing.

basicPropertyValues.val: Procedure used to identify the phototoxic potential of a test substance. The substance is administered either systemically or topically on the skin, and light is subsequently shone on the skin to photoexcite the substance.
Plant lectin that acts as a T-cell mitogen.
Animal antibody (or fragment thereof), expressed in a genetically modified plant.
Antibody-secreting plasma cell detected in vitro by its ability to produce a 'plaque' of lysed antigen-sensitized erythrocytes in the presence of complement.
Highly proliferative cell that is a developmental intermediate between small B lymphocytes and immunoglobulin (Ig)-secreting mature plasma cells.

comments: Plasma cells have eccentric nuclei, abundant cytoplasm, and distinct perinuclear haloes. The cytoplasm contains dense rough endoplasmic reticulum and a large Golgi complex.

basicPropertyValues.val: Terminally differentiated B lymphocyte, with little or no capacity for mitotic division, that actively secretes large amounts of antibody.
Dendritic cell of distinct lineage, found in blood and peripheral lymphoid tissue, which secretes large amounts of interferon (IFN) upon activation.
Mass of neoplastic monoclonal plasma cells growing in bone or soft tissue.

comments: Frequently used to remove antibodies in autoimmune disease.

basicPropertyValues.val: Technique of extracorporeal separation of blood cells from plasma, with return of the cells to the patient.
Small irregular or disc-shaped cell found in large numbers in mammalian blood, essential for blood clotting.

Alkyl phospholipid released by a variety of cell types including mast cells and basophils, which has immunoregulatory effects on lymphocytes and monocytes/macrophages, as well as causing platelet aggregation and degranulation.

comments: PDGF represents the major growth factor in human serum and is a potent mitogen for connective tissue and glial cells.

basicPropertyValues.val: Protein synthesized by platelets that is released into the serum during blood clotting.
Self-replicating cell capable of developing into cells and tissues of the three primary embryonic germ layers.
Plant lectin which is a T-cell-dependent B-cell mitogen.
Systemic disease characterized by widespread inflammation of small and medium-sized arteries in which many of the foci are nodular.
Substance that induces activation of multiple clones of B lymphocytes or T lymphocytes.

comments: (i) The autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 1 is characterized by mucocutaneous candidiasis in association with endocrine manifestation (also called APECED syndrome, autoimmune polyendocrinopathy-candidiasis-ectodermal dystrophy). (ii) The autoimmune polyglandular syndrome type 2 exhibits any combination of adrenal insufficiency (see Addison disease), diabetes mellitus type 1, lymphocytic thyroiditis (see thyroiditis, autoimmune), hypoparathyroidism, and gonadal failure.
In both types, organ-specific autoantibodies against a variety of endocrine glands are detectable.

basicPropertyValues.val: Autoimmune disease affecting multiple endocrine organs.
Polyinosinic:polycytidylic acid, a synthetic immunostimulant mimicking viral double-stranded RNA.
Polyinosinic:polycytidylic acid, poly-ʟ-lysine, and carboxymethylcellulose (letter roots of the acronym underlined), a synthetic immunostimulant mimicking viral double-stranded RNA.

Receptor molecule that specifically binds J chain-containing polymeric immunoglobulin (Ig), i.e., dimeric secretory immunoglobulin A (IgA) and pentameric immunoglobulin M (IgM), and transports it across mucosal epithelium.

comments: It is the predominating leukocyte in the blood and is found in the tissues during acute inflammatory processes and in the superficial surface aspects of a lesion during subacute or chronic inflammation.
There are three major types: neutrophils, eosinophils, and basophils.

basicPropertyValues.val: Mature leukocyte with granular cytoplasm and a segmented and irregularly shaped nucleus.
Disorder characterized by inflammation and degeneration of skeletal muscle, causing pain, weakness, and wasting in affected (usually proximal) muscles.
Test for immunosensitization measuring popliteal lymph node hyperplasia after subcutaneous injection of a test substance into the footpad of the hindpaw of a rodent.
Selection of those developing T cells in the thymus that are able to recognize self-major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules. This occurs by preventing apoptosis in these cells.

Cell in the B-lymphocyte lineage that has rearranged heavy chain but not light chain genes; it expresses surrogate light chains and \(\upmu\) heavy chain at its surface in conjunction with immunoglobulins Ig _012643_ and Ig _012644_. All these molecules comprise the pre-B-cell receptor (pre-BCR).
Antibody that is capable of reacting with a soluble antigen with the formation of an insoluble antigenantibody complex.
Precipitate of antibody and multivalent antigen due to the formation of high-molecular-weight complexes.

comments: During maturation thymocytes express on their surface a precursor T-cell receptor (TCR) called a pre-T-cell receptor, and both CD8 and CD4 proteins (double-positive cells). At the same time they slowly migrate from the outer cortex of the thymus to the inner medullary region. Only the \(\pu{2\%}\) of cells capable of distinguishing self-antigen survive to maturity in the medulla. Here they become single-positive cells, expressing exclusively CD4 or CD8 surface proteins, and are exported from the thymus in the bloodstream to become helper T cells (Th) and cytotoxic T cells, respectively.

basicPropertyValues.val: Cell differentiating into a T lymphocyte in the thymus gland.

comments: A positive result is far from conclusive and, at best, gives a vague indication of allergenicity. The prick test is inappropriate as a test for food allergens.

basicPropertyValues.val: Test carried out by placing a drop of a suspected allergenic extract on the skin of the forearm and gently pricking it into the upper layer of skin. Sensitivity to a substance is indicated if the spot swells slightly and becomes red within about \(\pu{15 min}\).

comments: Primary biliary cirrhosis-specific antibodies are antimitochondrial antibodies (AMAs) directed against proteins of the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex (mainly the E2 subunit).

basicPropertyValues.val: Autoimmune liver disease that results in the destruction of bile ducts, leading to fibrosis and cirrhosis.

comments: The primary response is generally weak, has a long induction phase or lag period, consists primarily of the release of immunoglobulin M (IgM) antibodies, and generates immunologic memory.

basicPropertyValues.val: Immune response to the first encounter with an antigen, characterized by slow production of antibody molecules and the priming of lymphoid tissue in readiness for the production of a secondary immune response on subsequent challenge with the same antigen.
First introduction of a vaccine into the body for the purposes of inducing immunity.
Region of a secondary lymphoid organ containing predominantly unstimulated B lymphocytes that develops into a germinal center following antigen stimulation.
Site at which immunocompetent lymphocytes develop, i.e., bone marrow and thymus in mammals.
Atrophic form of diffuse autoimmune thyroiditis.

comments: Often associated with ulcerative colitis [see inflammatory bowel disease (IBD)].

basicPropertyValues.val: Chronic, non-bacterial, inflammatory narrowing of the bile ducts.
Process of giving an initial sensitization to antigen.

comments: Other cells, e.g., fibroblasts and endothelial cells, that do not constitutively express major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class II molecules may be induced to do so by certain cytokines and are sometimes referred to as nonprofessional antigen-presenting cells.

basicPropertyValues.val: Highly efficient antigen-presenting cell (APC), generally referring to dendritic cells, B cells, or macrophages.

Systemic autoimmune disease marked by formation of hyalinized and thickened collagenous fibrous tissue, with thickening and adhesion of skin to underlying tissues, especially of the hands and face and vascular alterations.
Cytokine that initiates or enhances inflammation.
Any test that determines the effect on increase in cell number of a test agent such as a cytokine or mitogen.

comments: It migrates as a β3-globulin and, although not an antibody, may act in conjunction with complement-fixing antibody.

basicPropertyValues.val: Relatively heat-labile, normal serum protein (a euglobulin) that, in the presence of complement component C3 and magnesium ions, is involved in the alternative pathway of complement activation, and acts nonspecifically against Gram-negative bacteria and viruses and may contribute to the lysis of erythrocytes.

comments: Cytoplasmic proteasome is important in antigen processing and presentation by major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules.

basicPropertyValues.val: Cytoplasmic and nuclear multiprotein proteolytic complex involved in degradation of excess, damaged, or misfolded proteins.
Member of the Ly-6 family of cell surface molecules that prevents insertion of the membrane attack complex (MAC) into the membrane, thereby protecting cells from complement-induced lysis.
Protection against infectious agents conferred by vaccination.
Staphylococcus aureus cell wall protein that binds to the Fc region of immunoglobulin G (IgG).

comments: PR3 autoantibodies are diagnostic markers for Wegener granulomatosis (WG) and are involved in the pathogenesis of this disease. They are also found in patients with other autoimmune systemic vasculitic diseases.

basicPropertyValues.val: Multifunctional enzyme of azurophilic granules of neutrophils and monocytes and the major target of antineutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibodies (ANCA).
Streptococcal cell wall protein that binds to the Fc region of immunoglobulin G (IgG), with a wider species specificity than protein A.

comments: It is activated during B-lymphocyte and T-lymphocyte activation.

basicPropertyValues.val: Member of a kinase family with broad substrate specificity, activated by calcium, diacylglycerol, and (or) phorbol 12-myristate 13-acetate (PMA).

Loss of immunoprecipitation or agglutination that occurs when antibody concentration is increased to an extent that the antibody is in such excess that it is no longer able to effectively cross-link the antigen. A similar phenomenon may occur in antigen excess.

comments: Causes include direct histamine release and/or complement activation.

basicPropertyValues.val: Inflammatory or anaphylactic reaction with symptoms similar to an allergy but not involving an antigen-specific immune response, e.g., salicylate intolerance, reaction to contrast reagents.

comments: Psoriasis is associated with excessively rapid proliferation of keratinocytes which mature in less than a week.

basicPropertyValues.val: Skin disorder that has a hereditary component and is characterized by erythematous patches covered with silvery scales, especially on the elbows, knees, and scalp.
Of, relating to, or associated with psoriasis; affected with psoriasis.
Partially purified derivative of tuberculin used in the Mantoux test for tuberculosis.
Purple discoloration occurring in patches on the skin, mucus membranes, or organs.
Any of various tests used to determine whether an agent, usually an infusion or injection fluid, is free of pyrogens.
'Non-classical' major histocompatibility complex (MHC) class I molecule in mice.
Method for quantifying an antigen by measuring the diameters of circular precipitates around an antigen-spiked cavity in an antibody-containing agar gel.
Solid-phase radioimmunoassay (RIA) for detecting immunoglobulin E (IgE) antibody specific for a particular antigen.
Biochemical conjugate consisting of an immune-targeting molecule such as an antibody or antibody fragment together with a cytotoxic radionuclide.

comments: It is brought on characteristically by cold or emotional stimuli and relieved by heat, and may be due to an underlying disease or anatomic abnormality.

The phenomenon is more common in women than men and occurs in most patients with progressive systemic sclerosis (SSc), mixed connective tissue disease (MCTD), and polymyositis/scleroderma overlap syndrome.
When the condition is idiopathic or primary, it is termed Raynaud disease.

basicPropertyValues.val: Intermittent bilateral attacks of vasospasm and ischemia of the fingers or toes and sometimes of the ears and nose, marked by a severe pallor and often accompanied by paresthesia and pain.
Syndrome characterized by reversible airflow limitation and complicating bronchial hyperresponsiveness induced by acute exposure to high concentrations of non-sensitizer irritant gases.
Intermediates in the reduction of molecular dioxygen, \(\ce{O2}\), to water.
Historic term for antibodies of the immunoglobulin E (IgE) class.
Substance recognized by memory cells that stimulates rapid (secondary) immune responses, often associated with hypersensitivity.
Antibody fragment manufactured by use of genetically modified microorganisms.
Gene whose products are involved in V(D)J recombination in B cells and T cells. Two such genes that have been identified are RAG-1 and RAG-2.

Any conserved heptamer (7-nucleotide)-nonamer (9-nucleotide) sequence, separated by a 12 or 23 base spacer, which occurs 3′ of variable gene segments, 5′ and 3′ of diversity gene segments, and 5′ of joining gene segments, in both immunoglobulin (Ig) and T-cell receptor (TCR) genes. It functions as a recognition sequence for the recombinase enzymes that mediate the gene rearrangement process involved in the generation of lymphocyte antigen receptor diversity.
Parenchymal tissue of the spleen consisting of cords of cells and sinuses infiltrated with erythrocytes and responsible for removal of aged or damaged erythrocytes.
Large transformed lymphocyte, often binucleate, considered pathognomonic of Hodgkin lymphoma.

nodes.lbl: regulated upon activation normal T cell expressed and secreted

basicPropertyValues.val: Chemokine secreted by T cells and macrophages upon stimulation by mitogens, which acts as a chemoattractant and stimulates eosinophils and basophils.
Antibody or T-cell receptor (TCR) idiotope capable of regulating immune responses via interaction with lymphocytes bearing complementary idiotopes (anti-idiotopes).

T cell that controls the maintenance of normal immune homeostasis. Treg cells are involved in controlling (anergizing or counter-regulating) autoreactive cells that escaped from thymic negative selection.
Immune response leading to destruction of a transplanted organ or tissue.
Generation of cytotoxic superoxide from dioxygen due to increased NADPH oxidase activity, typically occurring in activated neutrophils.
Test of the ability of a substance to induce hyperreactivity in the airways, typically measured as an increase in the rate of respiration of guinea pigs during inhalation of the substance.

High-throughput procedure where information on potential immunogenic tumor proteins is gained from the amino acid sequences of gene products specifically expressed by the tumor, followed by predicted fitting of putative antigenic peptides to a peptide-binding groove, and finally experimental verification.
Inflammatory disease that may develop following a streptococcal infection such as strep throat, and may affect the heart, joints, skin, and brain.

comments: It primarily affects the joints, causing symmetrical lesions and severe damage to the affected joints. RA is the most common form of inflammatory joint disease (prevalence about \(\pu{0.5}\) to \(\pu{1\%}\)).

basicPropertyValues.val: Episodic inflammatory systemic disease with autoimmune pathogenetic mechanisms.

comments: Although detectable in various diseases, rheumatoid factor is used as a classification criterion of rheumatoid arthritis (RA).

basicPropertyValues.val: Immunoglobulins IgM, IgG, and IgA autoantibodies to the Fc region of IgG.
Inflammation of the mucous membrane of the nose.
Nasal discharge resulting from an allergic response.
Technique in which a test antigen is electrophoretically driven through an antibody-containing gel. The rocket-shaped tails of precipitation give information on the antigen concentration.
Particles or cells bound to the surface of a lymphocyte (e.g., sheep erythrocytes around a human T cell).
Single-chain molecule composed of the variable (V) regions of an antibody heavy and light chain joined together by a flexible linker.

comments: There is usually diminished or absent reactivity to tuberculin, and in most active cases, a positive Kveim reaction.

basicPropertyValues.val: Chronic, progressive, generalized granulomatous reticulosis of unknown etiology, involving almost any organ or tissue, including the skin, lungs, lymph nodes, liver, spleen, eyes, and small bones of the hands and feet. It is characterized histologically by the presence in all affected organs or tissues of noncaseating epithelioid cell tubercles.
Cell surface receptor, for example on phagocytes, which recognizes cells or molecules that require clearance from the body.

comments: There are two types: progressive systemic sclerosis, and a more limited and less rapidly progressive form known as CREST syndrome, referring to Calcinosis, Raynaud phenomenon, Esophageal dysfunction, Sclerodactyly, and Telangiectasias.

basicPropertyValues.val: Chronic progressive autoimmune disease characterized by systemic fibrosis and vascular changes.
Second exposure of primed lymphocytes to a given antigen.
Qualitatively and quantitatively improved immune response that occurs upon the second encounter of primed lymphocytes with a given antigen.
Tissue (organ) in which antigen-driven proliferation and differentiation of mature B and T lymphocytes take place following antigen recognition.
Accelerated rejection of an allograft in a primed recipient.
Proteolytic cleavage product of the poly-Ig receptor which remains associated with dimeric immunoglobulin A (IgA) in sero-mucus secretions.
Dimeric immunoglobulin A (IgA) found in sero-mucus secretions.
Any member of a family of cell-surface adhesion molecules found on leukocytes and endothelial cells and that bind to sugars on glycoproteins.

comments: Autoimmunity is the most prevalent manifestation of this deficiency. Individuals with SIgAD have an increased risk of developing systemic [e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), rheumatoid arthritis (RA)] and organ-specific (e.g., celiac disease) autoimmune disorders.

basicPropertyValues.val: Most common form of primary immunodeficiency.

comments: Breaking self-tolerance may lead to pathological autoimmunity and development of autoimmune disease.

Primary (clonal deletion, anergy, clonal indifference) and secondary or regulatory (interclonal competition, suppression, immune deviation, vetoing, feedback regulation by the idiotypic network) mechanisms are involved in the induction and maintenance of self-tolerance.

basicPropertyValues.val: Specific immunological unresponsiveness to a defined autoantigen.
Spread of bacteria or bacterial products throughout the blood, eliciting a life-threatening, systemic inflammatory reaction.
The appearance in the blood serum of detectable antibodies against a specific infectious agent.
Study of serum, especially blood serum, frequently used to detect antibodies to microorganisms.
Hypersensitive reaction to the administration of a foreign serum, characterized by fever, swelling, skin rash, and enlargement of the lymph nodes.
Immunodeficiency affecting both T and B lymphocytes.
T-cell-dependent target antigen often used in hemolytic plaque assays of immune responsiveness.

comments: Most are associated with cells of the immune system.

basicPropertyValues.val: Any member of a large family of lectins that bind sialylated glycans.

Any sequence of amino acid residues that, when linked to a newly synthesized protein, identifies it to transport mechanisms that guide the protein to a specific location among the organelles of a eukaryotic cell, or from the cytoplasm to the periplasmic space of prokaryotic cells.

nodes.lbl: signal transducer and activator of transcription

basicPropertyValues.val: Any member of a family of cytoplasmic proteins that act as second messengers to activate gene transcription in response to cytokines and growth factors.
Small antibody construct in which the variable fragment (Fv) [see variable (V) region] of a heavy chain is linked via a synthetic peptide to the variable fragment of a light chain.

comments: Two types of Sjögren syndrome are distinguished: a primary (isolated) type and a secondary type associated with another underlying autoimmune disease [e.g., RA, systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), systemic sclerosis (SSc), primary biliary cirrhosis (PBC), autoimmune hepatitis (AIH), multiple sclerosis, autoimmune thyroiditis, etc.]. Ro/SS-A and La/SS-B autoantibodies are used as classification criteria.

basicPropertyValues.val: Chronic inflammation of the lachrymal and salivary glands, often accompanied by rheumatoid arthritis (RA) and the presence of autoantibodies in the blood, occurring chiefly among women.
Skin-associated cells that participate in an immune response, including Langerhans cells, dendritic cells, and keratinocytes (mainly responsible for production of cytokines).
Any test used to study skin hypersensitivity such as the guinea pig maximization test or the Buehler test.
Procedure for evaluating immunity status, involving the introduction of a reagent into or under the skin.
Group of leukotrienes released by mast cells during anaphylaxis, which induces a prolonged contraction of smooth muscle.
Any member of a family of monomeric G proteins, with molecular mass typically \(\pu{20\!{-}\! 40 kDa}\), that also bind guanine nucleotides and are involved in signal transduction.
Protein from the shell of the bacteriophage T4, commonly used in construction of phage antibody libraries.
Theory that very few immunoglobulins (Ig) are inherited, but that extensive antibody diversity arises from mutations in non-reproductive cells.

comments: This exchange is a mechanism for generating a diverse immunoglobulin (Ig) repertoire in many non-human species.

basicPropertyValues.val: Nonreciprocal exchange of nucleic acid sequences between genes in which part of the donor gene or genes is 'copied' into an acceptor gene, but only the acceptor gene is altered.
Process giving rise to increased antibody diversity by cutting and splicing immunoglobulin (Ig) genes during lymphocyte differentiation.

comments: The spleen traps damaged erythrocytes carried in the blood.

basicPropertyValues.val: Largest of the secondary lymphoid organs, composed of white pulp, rich in lymphoid cells, and red pulp, which contains many erythrocytes and macrophages.
Of, pertaining to, connected with, or situated in the spleen.

Test for allergic contact dermatitis in which guinea pig skin is exposed to repeated applications of a test substance and intradermal injections of complete Freund’s adjuvant are administered separately.

Autoimmune thyroiditis (see thyroiditis, autoimmune) that develops spontaneously (without any apparent cause or manipulation) in certain strains of mice and rats (e.g., NOD mice, BB and BUF rats) as well as in other animals (e.g., OS chickens, marmoset monkeys, beagles).
Allergic reaction, often to a medication (see adverse drug reaction) or infection, characterized by blistering of the skin and ulceration of mucosal membranes.
Chronic remitting form of dermatitis characterized by severe photosensitivity and Ro/SS-A and La/SS-B autoantibodies.

Antigen which reacts with all the T cells belonging to a particular T-cell receptor (TCR) variable (V) region family, and which therefore stimulates (or deletes) a much larger number of cells than does conventional antigen.
Large group of proteins related by structural homology and function. The term also refers to the genes that encode them.

comments: The downregulation of responses to autoantigens is a major regulatory mechanism involved in the induction and maintenance of self-tolerance.

basicPropertyValues.val: Dominant immunological tolerance, a phenomenon that plays an active role in regulating T-cell and B-cell responses to both foreign antigens and autoantigens.
T cell that suppresses the immune response of B cells and other T cells to an antigen. In more current usage classified as a regulatory T cell.
Collection of molecules forming at the contact point of a T cell and an antigen-presenting cell (APC), enriched in T-cell receptor (TCR), adhesion molecules, and signaling molecules.

Light chain-like structure formed when the proteins encoded by the \({\rm{V}}_{\rm{preB}}\) and \(\uplambda_{5}\) genes associate with each other. It can form immunoglobulin (Ig)-like complexes which are expressed on the surface of pre-B cells at different stages of development.
Highly conserved repetitive sequence that mediates class switching in the immunoglobulin (Ig) heavy chain gene locus.
Autoimmune injury to one eye that occurs after penetrating injury or surgery to the other eye.

comments: A practical consequence is that cells can be transferred to other syngeneic animals without rejection.

basicPropertyValues.val: Genetically identical, e.g., a fully inbred strain of mice.
1) Relating to the body as a whole. 2) Occurring at a site in the body remote from the point of contact with a substance.
Autoimmune disease affecting a number of organs or tissues, or the whole body.

comments: SLE can affect any part of the body, but most often harms the heart, joints, skin, lungs, blood vessels, liver, kidneys, and nervous system. The course of the disease is unpredictable, with periods of illness (called flares) alternating with remission. SLE can occur at any age, and is most common in women, particularly of non-European descent.

The disease is very heterogeneous in clinical expression and serological factors. Autoantibodies directed against nuclear components [antinuclear antibodies (ANA)] are typically detected. Anti-dsDNA, anti-Sm, and antiphospholipid antibodies are used as classification criteria.

basicPropertyValues.val: Chronic autoimmune disease that is potentially debilitating and sometimes fatal as the immune system attacks the body’s cells and tissues, with inflammation and tissue damage.

comments: Anticentromere antibodies (ACA) as well as autoantibodies against DNA topoisomerase I (scl-70) and various nucleolar antigens are diagnostic and prognostic markers and are often detectable years before disease manifestation. They are also detectable in quartz dust-exposed individuals.
The skin ("scleroderma") and blood vessels (arteries, small vessels) are most commonly affected, but involvement of the lungs and gastrointestinal tract (esophagus) may also be observed.

basicPropertyValues.val: Fibrosing disease of unclear etiology that affects multiple organ systems.
T-memory cell that is specific for a drug allergen.
Immunotoxicity test that evaluates the ability of animals to produce antibodies to a T-dependent antigen [e.g., sheep red blood cells (SRBCs) or keyhole limpet hemocyanin (KLH)].

comments: Functional binding for TCR requires a complex of major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecule, antigenic peptide, and TCR.

basicPropertyValues.val: Antigen-specific receptor on T cells composed of one set of heterodimeric chains. Two types of TCR heterodimers are known (\(\upalpha/\upbeta\) and \(\upgamma/\updelta\)).
Antigen that requires helper T lymphocytes (Th) in order to elicit an antibody response.

nodes.lbl: TdT-dependent dUTP-biotin nick end labeling assay

basicPropertyValues.val: Method for detecting apoptotic cells in situ based on characteristic DNA fragmentation. It is based on the ability of terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) to transfer a labeled deoxyuridine triphosphate to the terminal ends arising from DNA cleavage.

comments: Th0-like responses are observed in patients with rheumatoid arthritis (RA), Sjögren syndrome, and Graves disease.

basicPropertyValues.val: Helper T lymphocyte (Th) with a less restricted cytokine profile than Th1 and Th2 cells.

comments: Th1-dominated responses are seen in autoimmune diseases in which cytotoxic T cells and macrophages play a major role, e.g., multiple sclerosis, diabetes mellitus type 1, Hashimoto thyroiditis, and Crohn disease. Switching from Th1 to Th2 response can prevent Th1-mediated tissue destruction in animal models.

basicPropertyValues.val: Helper T lymphocyte (Th) producing mainly interleukin-2 (IL-2), interferon (IFN-$\ce{\upgamma\!}$), and tumor necrosis factor $\ce{\upbeta\!}$ ($\ce{TNF\mbox{-}\upbeta\!}$), and thereby responsible for phagocyte-dependent host responses.

comments: Besides other effects, they provide optimal help for antibody responses. Th2 responses should also be regarded as an important downregulatory mechanism for exaggerated Th1 responses. Predominant Th2 cytokine profile is observed in patients with atopic disorders and graft-versus-host disease (GVHD).

basicPropertyValues.val: Helper T lymphocyte (Th) in mice producing interleukins IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-9, IL-10, and IL-13.
Helper T lymphocyte (Th) producing and responding to transforming growth factor $\ce{\upbeta\!}$ ($\ce{TGF\mbox{-}\upbeta\!}$) and helping immunoglobulin A (IgA) antibody responses.
Helper T lymphocyte (Th) producing interleukin IL-9, which stimulates mast cells.

comments: T17 lymphocytes are thought to play an important role in autoimmune disease.

basicPropertyValues.val: Helper T lymphocyte (Th), distinct from Th1 and Th2 cells, that secretes the interleukin IL-17.
Antigen that is able to elicit an antibody response in the absence of T cells.

comments: T-cell receptor (TCR) molecules are specific for complexes comprising short peptides bound to and presented by major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecules.

basicPropertyValues.val: Lymphocyte that matures in the thymus and has the ability to recognize specific peptide antigens through the receptors on its cell surface.

comments: It is abundant in the intestine and may be involved in tolerance to dietary antigens.

basicPropertyValues.val: T lymphocyte that regulates Th1 cell responses. It resembles the regulatory T cell (Treg) and is possibly related to the Th3 cell.

comments: Used in flow cytometry analysis.

basicPropertyValues.val: Molecular construct with two fluorochromes where the first excites the second by its emission.
Cell killed by one of the body’s killer cells, such as a cytotoxic T lymphocyte or natural killer (NK) cell.

Enzyme that inserts non-coded nucleotides at the junctions of V, D, and J gene segments of immunoglobulin (Ig) and T-cell receptor (TCR) locus DNA, thus increasing the diversity of antigen-specific recognition.
Detoxified tetanus toxin used to produce active immunity (see active immune response) against tetanus.

Technique used for selective staining of antigen-specific T lymphocytes in vitro or in situ. The antigen is presented to T cells by peptide tetramer constructs of major histocompatibility (MHC) class I molecules. It is also used to isolate antigen-specific T-cell populations for clonal expansion.
Ectopic lymphoid aggregates that accumulate during the process of chronic immune stimulation, and exhibit characteristics usually associated with the secondary lymphoid organs.

Any of several substances (predominantly thromboxanes A2 and B2) synthesized by platelets from arachidonic acid precursor, that cause vasoconstriction of vascular and bronchial smooth muscle and facilitates platelet aggregation.
Oral infection with Candida albicans, often in patients with immunosuppression.
Involution of the thymus gland leading to a diminished capacity to generate new T cells.
Process by which T cells, developing in the thymus, are screened for potentially harmful self-reactive T cells (which are removed), while potentially beneficial T cells are promoted.

comments: Thymoma is often associated with myasthenia gravis.

basicPropertyValues.val: Rare, usually benign, tumor arising from tissue of the thymus gland.
Antigen that requires the participation of T lymphocytes to elicit an immune response in B lymphocytes.
Antigen that does not require the participation of T lymphocytes to elicit an immune response in B cells.

comments: Thyroglobulin autoantibodies are found in patients with autoimmune thyroiditis, and Graves disease.

basicPropertyValues.val: Glycoprotein secreted by thyroid follicular cells that is a major autoantigen in autoimmune diseases of the thyroid.

comments: The most common types of autoimmune thyroiditis are Hashimoto thyroiditis and atrophic thyroiditis.

basicPropertyValues.val: Inflammatory destruction of the thyroid gland (ranging from a mild focal thyroiditis to extensive lymphocytic infiltration and scarring) often associated with goiter and hypothyroidism.

comments: Most TSHR autoantibodies are stimulatory, acting as agonists of thyroid-stimulating hormone, but receptor-blocking antibodies are also found.

basicPropertyValues.val: Main autoantigenic target in patients with Graves disease.
Thyroid enzyme that is a major autoantigen in autoimmune diseases of the thyroid.
Main target of autoantibodies in celiac disease.
Reciprocal of the highest dilution of a titration of an antigen with an antibody that gives a measurable effect (e.g., agglutination), and thus an empirical measure of the avidity of an antibody.

comments: Induction depends strongly on the circumstances of administration (e.g., route and concentration) in addition to any inherent property of the molecule.

basicPropertyValues.val: Member of a family of pattern recognition receptors involved in the detection of structures associated with pathogens or damaged host tissues.
A severe form of Stevens–Johnson syndrome with extensive detachment of the skin, often as a result of an allergic adverse drug reaction.

Systemic reaction produced by the toxin derived from the bacterium Staphylococcus aureus; the toxin acts as a superantigen, which activates a high proportion of CD4+ T lymphocytes to produce cytokines.
Chemically or physically modified toxin that is no longer harmful but retains immunogenicity.
Vesicular transport of macromolecules from one side of a cell to the other, through the cell’s interior.

comments: TGF-β is involved in several aspects of regulation of the immune system and blocks activation of lymphocytes and macrophages.

basicPropertyValues.val: Secreted member of the protein superfamily of the same name that functions in controlling the cell cycle and apoptosis.
Transference of blood or blood-based products from one individual into the circulation of another.
Grafting solid tissue (e.g., cornea) or organ (e.g., kidney or heart), or cells (particularly bone marrow), from one individual to another.
Molecules that carry antigenic peptides from the cytoplasm into the lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum for incorporation into major histocompatibility (MHC) class I molecules.
Essential amino acid for humans, and required for T-cell proliferation.
Antigen found in extracts of Mycobacteria, used in a skin test for tuberculosis (Mantoux test).

comments: Those who have been previously vaccinated with bacille Calmette–Guérin (BCG) also show a positive response.

basicPropertyValues.val: Diagnostic test in which antigens derived from the organism causing tuberculosis (Mycobacterium tuberculosis) are injected subcutaneously; individuals who have been exposed to the organism develop a delayed-type hypersensitivity (DTH) response at the injection site \(\pu{24}\) to \(\pu{48 h}\) later.
Antigen whose expression is associated with tumor cells.
Application of immunology to understanding tumor biology, immune system avoidance by tumors, and immunotherapy directed against tumors.
Mononuclear lymphocyte derived from the inflammatory infiltrate of a solid tumor.

comments: Activation of the \(\ce{TNF\mbox{-}\upalpha}\) receptor may trigger apoptosis through the extrinsic pathway.
It promotes the destruction of some types of cancer cells and is a cytokine involved in systemic inflammation.

basicPropertyValues.val: Protein produced and secreted by several of the body’s cell types, including leukocytes.
Family of proteins involved in regulating inflammation and apoptosis through interaction with the tumor necrosis factor receptor.
Antigen present specifically on a tumor cell that may target it for destruction by the immune system or for antibody therapy.
Antigen, present only on a tumor cell, and targetable by the immune system or by antibody therapy in order to destroy the tumor.

comments: Tyrosine kinases play a key role in lymphocyte activation. Major tyrosine kinases involved in T lymphocyte activation are Lck, Fyn, and ZAP-70; those involved in B lymphocyte activation are Blk, Fyn, Lyn, and Syk.

basicPropertyValues.val: Any member of a family of enzymes that phosphorylates target proteins on tyrosine residues, thus playing a crucial role in signal transduction.
Highly conserved 76 amino acid peptide abundant in eukaryotic cells. Its covalent attachment to a protein by a ubiquitin ligase complex targets that protein for destruction by the proteasome.

comments: Unresponsiveness may be specific for a particular antigen (see tolerance), or broadly nonspecific as a result of damage to the entire immune system, for example, after whole-body irradiation.

basicPropertyValues.val: Inability to respond to an antigenic stimulus.

Preferential partnering of \(\ce{J\upalpha\ gene}\) segments with \(\ce{V\upalpha\ gene}\) segments during rearrangement in the T-cell receptor (TCR) gene, possibly following deletion of the \(\ce{V\updelta\ gene}\) region.

comments: Recombination occurs only once in a cell’s lifetime.
The conventional syntax V(D)J indicates that V and J genes code the light chain and all three genes code the heavy chain, the processes being VJ and VDJ recombination, respectively.

basicPropertyValues.val: Mechanism for generating antigen-specific receptors of T cells and B cells; it involves the joining of V, D, and J gene segments, mediated by the enzyme complex V(D)J recombinase, and products of the recombination-activating genes.
Immunization with a vaccine against a pathogen.

Gene, segment(s) of which rearrange together with diversity (D) gene and joining (J) gene segments in order to encode the variable (V) region amino acid sequences of immunoglobulins (Ig) and T-cell receptors (TCRs).

comments: The V region consists of two V domains, \({\rm{V}}_{\rm{L}}\) and \({\rm{V}}_{\rm{H}}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: N-terminal portion of an immunoglobulin (Ig) or T-cell receptor (TCR) that contains the antigen-binding region of the molecule. V regions are formed by the recombination of V(D) and J gene segments.
Cell adhesion molecule present on the luminal surface of blood and lymph vessel endothelium, recognized by homing molecules that direct leukocytes to tissues with the appropriate 'address'.
Molecule, expressed on the surface of endothelial cells that functions in the adhesion of lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, and basophils to vascular endothelium to the vascular surface.

comments: Vasculitis can lead to necrosis, fibrosis, or thrombosis. Autoimmunity plays an important role in some vasculitides (e.g., ANCA-associated vasculitis, Goodpasture syndrome, cryoglobulinemic vasculitis).

basicPropertyValues.val: Group of disorders that share a common underlying problem of inflammation of a blood vessel or vessels.
Substance containing amino group(s) that increases vascular permeability and smooth muscle contraction.
Specific antigen expressed on lymphocytes very soon after activation by phorbol myristate acetate (PMA).
T-cell surface antigen, named for its delayed appearance after T-cell activation; a member of the integrin superfamily involved in cell adhesion.
Elimination by apoptosis of a self-peptide-major histocompatibility complex (MHC) molecule recognizing lymphocyte by a self-peptide-presenting (veto) cell.
Autoantibodies that react optimally at higher temperatures (\(\pu{37^{\circ}C}\)) with surface antigens of erythrocytes. They mediate autoimmune hemolytic anemia.

comments: Necrotizing glomerulonephritis is common in WG.

basicPropertyValues.val: Granulomatous inflammation involving the respiratory tract, and necrotizing vasculitis affecting small to medium-sized vessels (e.g., capillaries, venules, arterioles, and arteries).
Circumscribed papule or plaque of edema of the skin, occurring as an urticarial lesion.

Dermatological reaction at a skin site where an antigen is injected into an allergic individual. The reaction is characterized by a 'flare' of erythema and a wheal produced by serum exuding into tissue, causing local edema.
Collections of lymphocytes in the spleen, responsible for its immune function.

Condition characterized by chronic eczema, chronic suppurative otitis media, anemia, and thrombocytopenic purpura (accompanied by bloody diarrhea); it is an immunodeficiency syndrome transmitted as an X-linked recessive trait, in which there is poor antibody response to polysaccharide antigens and dysfunction of cell-mediated immunity.
Sex-linked impairment of the ability to produce mature B cells, thus characterized by recurrent infections.

Sex-linked trait carried on the X-chromosome of severe combined immunodeficiency syndrome resulting from nonfunctional B lymphocytes and lack of T lymphocytes and natural killer (NK) lymphocytes, leading to recurrent, persistent, and severe infections.
Tissue or organ graft between individuals of different species.
Autophagy selective for degradation of intracellular bacteria and viruses.
T-lymphocyte-specific tyrosine kinase involved in T-lymphocyte activation.

Crude preparation of yeast cell walls, consisting chiefly of polysaccharide, activating the alternative pathway of the complement system in the presence of properdin and used in the immunoassay of this compound.

comments: Depending upon the nature of the solvent, the solvophilic and solvophobic parts of the molecule may be ionic or non-ionic moieties.

The term is most commonly applied to molecules in aqueous media within which the existence of distinct polar (hydrophilic) and nonpolar (hydrophobic) regions in the molecule promotes the formation of micelles, vesicles, or aggregates.

basicPropertyValues.val: Substance made up of molecules containing groups that are solvophilic and other groups that are solvophobic with respect to a given solvent.
Amphiphile, the constituent molecules of which have solvophilic groups at each end of a solvophobic chain.
Mesophase formed by varying the pressure at constant temperature.
Having a rod- or lath-like shape.
Host-guest complex formed by a carcerand and a completely entrapped guest.
Host molecule that completely entraps a guest molecule.
Self-assembly of two or more self-assembling species that might or might not incorporate a non-assembling component into an ordered structure.

comments: A coil-to-globule transition is the reverse of a globule-to-coil transition.
Typical external stimuli may be temperature, \(\pu{pH}\), electrolyte concentration, or solvent composition.

basicPropertyValues.val: Change in conformation of a macromolecular chain in solution from that of a coil to a relatively compact structure in which the chain has collapsed upon itself in response to an external stimulus.
Two- or three-dimensional ordered array of molecules or nanoparticles having a dimension roughly between \(\pu{1 nm}\) and \(\pu{1 \upmu m}\) in at least one direction.

comments: A columnar assembly of discotic molecules, called a columnar mesophase, a columnar discotic mesophase, or a columnar discotic, is one of the class of liquid crystal mesophases.

basicPropertyValues.val: Cylindrical assembly of molecules within a distinct series of layers in which the axes of the molecules lie in the planes of the layers and are identically aligned and oriented in adjacent layers.

comments: Such structures are used, for example, for drug delivery and dye or adulterant encapsulation.
The amphiphiles are often amphiphilic block copolymers

basicPropertyValues.val: Core-shell structure formed by self-assembly of amphiphiles and subsequently covalently crosslinked through functionalities in the core.
Molecular entity of spherical, elliptical, or cylindrical symmetry in which the constitution of the interior, the core, differs from that of the external surface, the shell.

comments: In this context, the terms are commonly shortened to "defect".

basicPropertyValues.val: Interruption to the regular pattern of atomic arrangement in crystal lattices.
Pertaining to assemblies of atoms, molecules, or ions with an overall three-dimensional order of cubic symmetry.
Mesophase with an overall three-dimensional order of cubic symmetry.

comments: In uniaxial nematics, formed by compounds consisting of either rod- or disc-like molecules, the mean direction of the effective molecular symmetry axis coincides with the director.
The director also coincides with a local symmetry axis of any directional property of the mesophase, such as the refractive index or magnetic susceptibility.
The director is defined as a unit vector, but directions \(\boldsymbol{+n}\) and \(\boldsymbol{-n}\) are arbitrary.

basicPropertyValues.val: Local symmetry axis for the singlet, orientational distribution of the molecules of a mesophase.

comments: The adjective "discotic" is also employed to describe the nematic mesophases formed by discotic mesogens. The mesophases formed by a columnar stacking of disc-like molecules are described as columnar mesophases.

basicPropertyValues.val: Mesogen composed of relatively flat, disc- or sheet-shaped molecules.

Assembly or supramolecular assembly, the components of which are linked through reversible bondings that enable structural reassembly by reshuffling in response to changes in the chemical or physical environment.
Polymer with constitutional units that are susceptible to a change in orientation under the influence of an electric field that causes the system to have induced polarity.
Confinement of microscopic particles with a host.
Confinement of an individual molecule within a larger molecule.

comments: Fields include electromagnetic, hydrodynamic, mechanical, etc.

basicPropertyValues.val: Field surrounding a molecular or ionic species emanating from a source external to that species.
Qualifier indicating attraction to fluorous compounds.
Qualifier indicating repulsion by fluorous compounds.
Repulsive interaction of fluorous and non-fluorous structures.
Pertaining to the presence of a sufficient number of carbon-fluorine bonds as to cause a substance to be insoluble in water or common organic solvents but soluble in fluorocarbons.

comments: A helix, \(\ce{\upbeta\mbox{-}sheet}\), or globule are typical secondary structures.

basicPropertyValues.val: Polymer or oligomer molecule that adopts a secondary structure stabilized by noncovalent interactions.
Conformation of a macromolecule in which the constitutional units collectively arrange into a compact ovoid or spherical shape.
Complex formed by a hemicarcerand and an entrapped guest.
Host molecule that allows guest molecules to enter and exit its cavities in accordance with a change in the equilibrium conditions.
Columnar mesophase characterized by a hexagonal packing of the molecular column.

comments: A method that utilizes the condensation of micrometer-size water droplets on the surface of solutions of block copolymers for the preparation of ordered micrometer-size honeycomb structures has led to the use of the extended term, honeycomb polymer from breath figures.
The cross-sectional dimensions of the holes of a hexagonal array are usually less than \(\pu{1 mm}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: Hexagonal array of holes in a polymer film.
Attractive interaction between hydrophilic groups, molecules, or substances.

comments: Literally translated as "water hating".

basicPropertyValues.val: Qualifier indicating capacity of a molecular entity or of a substituent to interact repulsively with polar molecules, in particular with water or with polar groups.

comments: An inverse opal is usually produced by assembling spheres, filling the interstitial spaces with solid, and removing the spheres.

basicPropertyValues.val: Colloidal crystal of spherical voids with a periodic structure within a solid polymer continuum.
Organized structure extended in two dimensions and of uniform thickness resembling a thin layer, a plate, or a membrane.

comments: Individual lamellae are usually of a thickness of \(\pu{5\!-\! 100 nm}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: Assembly of block copolymer molecules in which like blocks are segregated in lamella.

comments: Layer-by-layer assembly is often used to alternately transfer polyelectrolytes that are positively and negatively charged.
The material at the liquid surface need not necessarily be present as a solid monolayer.

basicPropertyValues.val: Process whereby multilayered structures of molecules or particles of a substance are assembled on a solid substrate by sequential adsorption of monolayers held together by noncovalent interactions.
Supramolecular structure in which molecules are linked only as a consequence of their topology.
Mesogen composed of molecules incorporating one or more metal atoms.
Rod-like mesogens with the capacity to form micellar aggregates.
Structure of material in which at least one of the features repeats over distances of the order of micrometers.
Technique to create templated cavities in polymer matrices with memory of the template molecules to be used in molecular recognition.
Region of a self-assembled entity with an equivalent diameter of approximately \(\pu{(1\!-\! 100) nm}\).
Polymer film that has lateral dimensions in the range of \(\pu{(1\!-\! 100) nm}\).

comments: The term is especially used of colloids that form solvates in organic solvents and thereby swell.

basicPropertyValues.val: Qualifier indicating tendency of a molecular entity or of a pendent group thereof to interact favourably with nonpolar organic solvents.
Attractive interaction between organophilic molecules or materials.
Order parameter applied to macroscopic assemblies of ordered materials, such as crystal assemblies in fibers.

comments: A polymeric branch may be termed a "ong-chain branch".
An oligomeric branch may be termed a "short-chain branch".

basicPropertyValues.val: Oligomeric or polymeric offshoot from a macromolecular chain.

comments: Most reported polymersomes serve as hosts for an aqueous solution and are useful for the accommodation or temporary trapping of molecules such as drugs, enzymes, and other proteins and peptides in in vivo applications.

basicPropertyValues.val: Vesicle with radius ranging from \(\pu{50 nm}\) to greater than \(\pu{5 \upmu m}\) constructed from an amphiphilic synthetic block copolymer.

comments: A polyrotaxane may also be composed of macromolecules comprising one or more macrocyclic main-chain or side-chain units threaded with linear chains.
The macrocycle(s) may be threaded onto the polymer backbone or side-chains.

basicPropertyValues.val: Polymer comprising mechanically interlocked molecular architectures typically of a macromolecule threaded through one or more macrocycles.

comments: Ditopic receptors can be either homotopic or heterotopic according to whether or not the binding sites are the same (typically, self-complementary binding sites) or different.

basicPropertyValues.val: Copolymer the molecules of which consist of rigid and flexible blocks.

comments: The Scatchard equation is \[\frac{r}{c} = -K_{\rm{a}} r + K_{\rm{a}} n\] in which \(r\) is the ratio of the concentration of bound ligand to the concentration of available protein binding sites, \(c\) is the concentration of free ligand, and \(n\) is the number of binding sites per protein molecule.
The association constant, \(K_{\rm{a}}\), has units of reciprocal concentration.

basicPropertyValues.val: Equation used to calculate the association constant, \(K_{\rm{a}}\), of a ligand with a protein molecule.
Linear plot of \(r/c\) against \(r\) in accordance with the Scatchard equation.
Inter- or intra-molecular self-assembly of constitutional units within the backbones of polymer molecules.
Inter- or intra-molecular self-assembly of side-chains or constitutional units of polymer molecules.

comments: Such structures are used, e.g., in drug delivery and dye encapsulation.
The amphiphiles are often amphiphilic block copolymers.

basicPropertyValues.val: Core-shell structure formed by self-assembly of amphiphiles and subsequently covalently crosslinked through functionalities in the shell.
Pertaining to the arrangement and orientation of molecules in a smectic mesophase.

comments: Although the total number of smectic mesophases cannot be specified, the following types have been defined: \(SmA\), \(SmB\), \(SmC\), \(SmF\), and \(SmI\). The alphabetical order of suffixes merely indicates an order of discovery.
Smectic mesophases are amongst the class of liquid-crystal mesophases.
There are several types of smectic mesophases, characterised by a variety of molecular arrangements within the layers.

basicPropertyValues.val: Mesophase that has the molecules arranged in layers with a well-defined layer spacing or periodicity.
Macrocyclic compound capable of completely enveloping a cation, having donor atoms (\(\ce{O}\), \(\ce{N}\), \(\ce{S}\)) arranged such that they provide a solvation sphere to the encapsulated cation.

comments: \(\ce{\uppi\mbox{-}\uppi}\) Interactions become stronger as the number of \(\ce{\uppi\mbox{-}electrons}\) increases.

basicPropertyValues.val: Inter- or intra-molecular alignment of aromatic groups within molecules induced by the interactional overlap of their \(\ce{\uppi\mbox{-}orbitals}\).

comments: T-stacking is often seen in proteins where the partially positively charged hydrogen atom of one aromatic system points to the centre of the aromatic plane of another aromatic system.

basicPropertyValues.val: Orthogonal alignment of constitutional units within molecules that lead to favourable interactions.

comments: The external stimuli might be temperature, incident radiation, \(\pu{pH}\), etc., and responses would be manifest as changes in a physical property such as conformation, aggregation, liquid-crystalline state, absorption spectrum, emission spectrum, etc.

basicPropertyValues.val: Polymer that responds reversibly to external stimulus or stimuli.
Qualifier indicating an affinity for solvents.
Qualifier indicating a lack of affinity for solvents.

comments: Use of the term "supramolecular polymerization" is discouraged.

basicPropertyValues.val: Self-assembly involving reversible, noncovalent, directional interactions of molecules that result in a high-molecular-mass entity.

Polymerization of monomer molecules adsorbed and oriented (a) on a surface, (b) in a polymer lattice, (c) on polymer molecules in solution, or (d) round a metal ion whereby the structure of the polymer chains formed is controlled by the orientation of the monomer molecules.

comments: Liposomes have potential use in drug delivery.

basicPropertyValues.val: Vesicle constructed from a lipid bilayer.
Qualifier for something that is made by human activity, rather than occurring naturally.

comments: Artificial polymer should also be used in the case of chemically modified biopolymers.
Biochemists are now capable of synthesizing copies of biopolymers that should be named synthetic biopolymers to make a distinction with true biopolymers.
Genetic engineering is now capable of generating non-natural analogues of biopolymers that should be referred to as artificial biopolymers, e.g., artificial protein, artificial polynucleotide, etc.

basicPropertyValues.val: Man-made polymer that is not a biopolymer.

comments: This definition is derived from "material which has been designed to induce specific biological activity" and is limited to material made bioactive on purpose. However, the concept of bioactivity does not imply beneficial action only, although the term is often used positively, i.e., to reflect a beneficial action.

basicPropertyValues.val: Qualifier for a substance that provokes any response from a living system.

comments: Stealth is often used to reflect the absence of recognition by defense proteins of the complement, and more generally opsonins that serve as binding enhancers for the process of phagocytosis.

There is no polymer (solid or in solution) that is inert in contact with a living system, because of adsorption and/or physical-chemical interactions with life elements (biopolymers, cells, and tissues).

basicPropertyValues.val: Capability of a substance, such as a drug or a vaccine, to provoke a response from a living matter.

comments: Assessing of adhesion is made after washing to eliminate unattached cells.
Cell adhesion is generally followed by proliferation as a biofilm or as a tissue.
The use of the term "bioattachment" is discouraged.

basicPropertyValues.val: Adhesion of cells or tissues to the surface of a material.
Cell-mediated chemical modification without main chain scission.

comments: In vitro activity of isolated enzymes cannot be considered as biological activity.

basicPropertyValues.val: Capability of being degraded by biological activity.
Disintegration resulting from the action of cells.

comments: A biofilm is a fixed system that can be adapted internally to environmental conditions by its inhabitants.
The self-produced matrix of EPS, which is also referred to as slime, is a polymeric conglomeration generally composed of extracellular biopolymers in various structural forms.

basicPropertyValues.val: Aggregate of microorganisms in which cells that are frequently embedded within a self-produced matrix of extracellular polymeric substance (EPS) adhere to each other and/or to a surface.
Fragmentation resulting from the action of cells.

comments: The definition "non-viable material used in a medical device, intended to interact with biological systems" recommended in cannot be extended to the environmental field where people mean "material of natural origin".
The notion of exploitation includes utility for applications and for fundamental research to understand reciprocal perturbations as well.

This general term should not be confused with the terms biopolymer or biomacromolecule. The use of "polymeric biomaterial" is recommended when one deals with polymer or polymer device of therapeutic or biological interest.

basicPropertyValues.val: Material exploited in contact with living tissues, organisms, or microorganisms.

comments: Biomineralization is a process generally concomitant to biodegradation.

If the substance is involved in an application, the term has to be related to a desired duration of performance, because almost any material ages in contact with living systems and biochemical processes regardless of the domain.

basicPropertyValues.val: Resistance to the deleterious action of living systems that allows preservation of the initial characteristics of a substance.
Pertaining to, or produced by, living cells or organisms.

comments: Generally, degradation is faster inside because of autocatalysis by entrapped degradation byproducts or by the presence of a chain-cleaving reagent entrapped within the matrix.
The molar mass of the whole sample decreases progressively as opposed to the constancy observed in the case of erosion and bioerosion.

This expression is often used when degradation is faster inside than at the surface. This is not appropriate. Nevertheless, it should be adopted specifically in opposition to erosion. In this case, the molar mass distribution becomes rapidly bimodal.

basicPropertyValues.val: Homogeneous degradation affecting the volume of a sample.

comments: If only a delayed or prolonged release is obtained without matching a desired release profile, the expression sustained delivery is to be used.

basicPropertyValues.val: Supply of a substance according to desired rate and amount over time.
Macromolecule that is able to undergo chain scissions under specific conditions, resulting in a decrease of molar mass.
Polymer in which macromolecules are able to undergo chain scissions, resulting in a decrease of molar mass.

comments: The process of degradation may be specified by a prefix or an adjective preceding the term "degradation". For example, degradation caused by the action of water is termed "hydrodegradation" or hydrolysis; by visible or ultraviolet light is termed "photodegradation"; by the action of oxygen or by the combined action of light and oxygen is termed "oxidative degradation" or "photooxidative degradation", respectively; by the action of heat or by the combined effect of chemical agents and heat is termed "thermal degradation" or "thermochemical degradation", respectively; by the combined action of heat and oxygen is termed "thermooxidative degradation".

basicPropertyValues.val: Progressive loss of the performance or of the characteristics of a substance or a device.

comments: Adapted where the definition is general. For biorelated polymers, the definition is purposely and specifically limited to the chemical degradation of macromolecules in order to make a clear distinction with the physical degradation of the material.
Degradation can result from the action of enzymes (see enzymatic degradation), or from the action of cells, organisms, and/or microorganisms.
In any condition, degradation must be used instead of biodegradation when the mechanism of chain scission is not known or demonstrated as cell-mediated.

basicPropertyValues.val: Degradation that results in desired changes in the values of in-use properties of the material because of macromolecule cleavage and molar mass decrease.
Mass fraction of a substance that is bioassimilated.

comments: Expressions like degree of biodegradability, extent of biodegradability, etc., are improper because a property reflected by the suffix "ity" cannot be quantified contrary to a deed reflected by "tion".

basicPropertyValues.val: Mass fraction of a substance that is biodegraded under specified conditions as measured through specified phenomena or techniques sensitive to mineral and biomass formations.
Mass fraction of a biodisintegrated substance.
Mass fraction of the original material that is biofragmented.
Mass fraction of a substance that is biomineralized.
Mass fraction of a polymer that is degraded under specified conditions as measured through a specified phenomenon sensitive to molecular dimensions.

comments: The size is generally defined by sieving. It is a practical characteristic in composting.

basicPropertyValues.val: Mass fraction of the particles of defined size issued from a fragmented substance.
Mass fraction of a substance that is fragmented.
Mass fraction of a substance that is mineralized.

comments: A depolymerase does not necessarily convert all the macromolecules to monomer molecules, occasionally, a specific oligomer is the end-product, depending on the mechanism.
This term is generally used in the case of macromolecules produced by bacteria, because bacteria have the potential to degrade the biopolymers they synthesized.

basicPropertyValues.val: Enzyme that is able to catalyse the depolymerization of a biomacromolecule.

comments: Deterioration can result from physical and/or chemical phenomena.
Deterioration is connected to a loss of performances and thus to the function, whereas degradation is connected with a loss of properties.
Polymer deterioration is more general than polymer degradation, which reflects loss of properties resulting from chemical cleavage of macromolecules only.

basicPropertyValues.val: Deleterious alteration of a material in quality, serviceability, or vigor.

comments: The limiting size is generally defined according to sieving conditions.

basicPropertyValues.val: Fragmentation to particles of a defined size.
Ability of a material to retain the values of its properties under specified conditions.

comments: Degradation caused by enzymes can be observed under biotic or abiotic conditions but only degradation due to cell bioactivity can be called biodegradation, otherwise enzymatic degradation is to be used, especially in the case of in vitro abiotic conditions.
Sometimes called enzymic degradation.

basicPropertyValues.val: Degradation caused by the catalytic action of enzymes.

comments: Erosion can also result from chemical degradation when the degrading reagent reacts faster than it diffuses inside. There is a risk of confusion that can be eliminated after careful and detailed investigation of the degradation mechanism. (See bioerosion.)

See enzymatic degradation. In the case of polymers, water-soluble enzymes can hardly diffuse into the macromolecular network, except, maybe, in some hydrogels. They adhere to surfaces to cause erosion.
The wording bulk erosion is incorrect and its use therefore discouraged.

basicPropertyValues.val: Degradation that occurs at the surface and progresses from it into the bulk.
Process of inserting new genetic information into existing cells in order to modify a specific organism for the purpose of changing its characteristics.

comments: Not to be confused with ultimate degradation.
This expression reflects the fact that some biodegradable parts of a biodegradable material may not be accessible to biodegradation.

basicPropertyValues.val: Greater value of the degree of biodegradation that can be reached under selected experimental conditions.

comments: The substances can be drugs, pesticides, dyes, etc.

basicPropertyValues.val: Hollow microparticle composed of a solid shell surrounding a core-forming space available to permanently or temporarily entrapped substances.

comments: The lower limit between micro- and nano-sizing is still a matter of debate. (See nanoparticle.)
To be consistent with the prefix "micro" and the range imposed by the definition, dimensions of microparticles should be expressed in \(\pu{\upmu\!m}\).

basicPropertyValues.val: Particle with dimensions between \(\pu{1E-7}\) and \(\pu{1E-4 m}\).

comments: The absence of outer layer forming a distinct phase is important to distinguish microspheres from microcapsules because it leads to first-order diffusion phenomena, whereas diffusion is zero order in the case of microcapsules.

basicPropertyValues.val: Microparticle of spherical shape without membrane or any distinct outer layer.

comments: A particular case is the process by which living organisms produce and structure minerals often to harden or stiffen existing tissues. (See biomineralization.)

In the case of polymer biodegradation, this term is used to reflect conversion to _015233_ and \(\ce{H2O}\) and other inorganics. \(\ce{CH4}\) can be considered as part of the mineralization process because it comes up in parallel to the minerals in anaerobic composting, also called methanization.

basicPropertyValues.val: Process through which an organic substance becomes impregnated by or turned into inorganic substances.
Hollow nanoparticle composed of a solid shell that surrounds a core-forming space available to entrap substances.

comments: A nanosphere is composed of a matrix where substances can be permanently or temporarily embedded, dissolved, or covalently bound.

basicPropertyValues.val: Nanoparticle of spherical shape without membrane or any distinct outer layer.

comments: The use of this term instead of polymer is a source of confusion and thus is not recommended.
This term is used in polymer engineering for materials often compounded that can be processed by flow.

basicPropertyValues.val: Generic term used in the case of polymeric material that may contain other substances to improve performance and/or reduce costs.

comments: In pharmaceutical preparations, incompatible polymer-drug mixtures are generally solid dispersions.
Solid dispersion is commonly prepared by three different methods, namely, solventbased, fusion-melt, and hybrid fusion-solvent methods.
The dispersed compounds can be in clusters of particles.
The nonpolymeric components can act as fillers.

basicPropertyValues.val: Solid multiphasic mixture with at least one polymer component dominating.

comments: The generated action can be unique or cyclic. It generally results from cooperative phenomena.
The stimulus can affect macromolecules or macromolecule assemblies forming the polymer.

basicPropertyValues.val: Polymer that responds or that is designed to respond to a stimulus like pH, light, heat, etc. change, and provides a predetermined action.

comments: In some cases, the container is a polymer processed as implant, film, microparticle, or nanoparticle, auto-assembly of molecules, or a macromolecule.
In the case of sustained delivery according to required specifications, the use of controlled delivery is recommended.
The substance can be temporarily embedded, dissolved, or covalently bound.
The term is relevant to the release of substances like pesticides, dyes, drugs, etc.

basicPropertyValues.val: Supply of a substance from a container where it is temporarily entrapped for the sake of achieving a prolonged action.
Copy of a biopolymer man-made using abiotic chemical routes.

comments: This expression is used as reference to assess biodegradable components that are not accessible to biodegradation from those that are bioavailable.

basicPropertyValues.val: Degree of biodegradation that corresponds to conversion of all the organic matter present in an original polymer-based item to minerals and biomass.

comments: The use of this expression is not recommended.
This term reflects the end-products of biodegradation. As such, it differs from the theoretical degree of biodegradation, which depends on the presence of non-biodegradable components.

basicPropertyValues.val: Complete breakdown of a compound to either fully oxidized or reduced simple molecules (such as carbon dioxide/methane, nitrate/ammonium, and water).
Medical device that replaces, in part or in whole, the function of one of the organs of the body.

comments: The term is relevant to therapy in surgery, medicine, pharmacology, dentistry, etc.

basicPropertyValues.val: Qualifier for a domain grouping scientific and practical activities related to therapy.
Implantable prosthesis that consists totally or substantially of nonviable, treated donor tissue.

comments: Bioassimilation with formation of novel biomass is a particular means of elimination often combined with the other pathways.
Natural pathways are kidneys through glomerular filtration and lungs after metabolization.

basicPropertyValues.val: Ability to be eliminated from an animal or human body through natural pathways.

comments: Bioresorption is now considered as pertinent and should be used specifically only when foreign material and residues have been shown assimilated or eliminated from the living host, regardless of the followed route, namely, lungs or kidneys or insertion in biochemical processes.
In the case of polymers or high-molar-mass macromolecules that are retained in parenteral compartments, degradation or biodegradation is necessary prior to bioresorption.

This concept does not apply to the environment as everything, including degradation by-products issued from outdoor degradation or biodegradation can only be stored or chemically transformed on Earth, so far.

basicPropertyValues.val: Disappearance of a substance from an organism by processes of metabolism, secretion, or excretion.

comments: In dentistry, polymer-based cements are also used as fillers of cavities. They are generally cured photochemically using UV radiation in contrast to bone cements.
